I said that he would seek a knock-out in 1942 on the Atlantic to cut Britain's life line. I referred also to the menace to the American continent' from the Atlantic and Pacific with perhaps an invasion of Canada from our front, side and back door. The extract I wish to read is from one of the most able papers in Great Britain, the National Review. I shall read just the relevant parts of this article which appeared in the February issue, page 121. The writer is the ablest man in this war; he has predicted everything that has happened so far. Referring to St. Pierre and Miquelon, he says:
Some weeks ago, Admiral Muselier, the commander of free French navy, did the allies the signal service of landing on St. Pierre and Miquelon, two French islands near Newfoundland, and taking them over in the name of General de Gaulle. He did this in response to a request from the inhabitants, who found themselves at odds with the Vichy officials who were still governing them. The sturdy descendants of Breton fishermen who live on the other side of the Atlantic had no mind to see their islands used against Canada and the British in the event of Vichy turning them over to Hitler.
Then follows reference to the same matter to which I referred, and the article continues:
During the ruthless German attack on our Atlantic shipping, it was criminal to leave such a nest for pirate-protection free to work its mischief. IV c do not know whether the attention of the British and American governments was called to what was going on. It seems probably that it was, for the activity of the Vichy friends of Germany was well known, not only to the fishermen on the islands-there are several thousands of them-but to the British in Newfoundland, barely twenty miles away. In any case nothing was done, the Monroe doctrine being invoked to defend inaction, while an agreement that there should be no disturbance of the American status quo during the war, was further used to produce inertia.
The last sentence reads:
Seeing that there would be no betterment in the affairs of their island from the two great powers, the inhabitants of St. Pierre and Miquelon appealed to General de Gaulle, who acted with military promptitude, and sent Admiral Muselier to seize the islands in the name of free France. This was done. The United States of America protested at once, and their press supported them, while certain elements in Canada were doubtful. A valuable passage in Mr. Churchill's Ottawa speech brushed away the anti-de Gaulle talk. The names of the Free French, he said, "will be held and are being held in increasing respect by nine Frenchmen out of every ten."

He lived here for years and got all the information.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: POLICY AS TO MAKING ANNOUNCEMENTS OF SINKINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to ask a question of the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services.
On May 12 the minister gave a statement to the press in relation to the sinking of a freighter in the St. Lawrence by enemy action. Yesterday the minister in reply to the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) further stated that a second ship had been sunk by enemy action in the same general locality at about the same time. In both statements the .minister indicated that in future it would be the policy of the department not to make any announcement of any further sinkings in this area, on the ground that to do so might convey valuable information to the enemy; that such information cannot and will not be given in answer to questions in the house or elsewhere and in no circumstances will it be given unless the government is satisfied that the enemy will not benefit therefrom.
In view of the fact that the enemy must have information of these sinkings, and that the government of the United States are announcing their losses from time to time, and that periodically Britain has announced similar losses, I desire to ask the minister to review this policy. I suggest to him that such a policy is not good for the morale of the people of Canada. They hear these stories, in most cases well authenticated. Now and hereafter the press is censored and the public is not allowed to know the truth, and the stories grow in repeating them. Isolated sinkings in the St. Lawrence estuary are not like the sinkings on the Atlantic or in the Mediterranean, or even in the far east, in which last named locality the reports of sinkings have been published at least in the United States and in Canada. Personally, I cannot conceive that the publication of true reports of these sinkings is of any particular value to the enemy or that the censorship now imposed will prevent the enemy from knowing of the sinkings.
Hon. ANGUS L. MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence for Naval Services): Mr. Speaker, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) gave me a copy of his question just before three o'clock, and in reply to what he has just said I must say that I see no reason whatever for changing the policy announced yesterday and the day before.
My hon. friend and the house will understand me when I say that if I were to begin to explain the reasons for the policy, that in itself might be of some aid and comfort to the enemy. If I said why we are withholding this information, or if I said when would be the proper time to announce a sinking, that explanation in itself might give information to the enemy.
The government of the United States, it i3 true, have released from time to time news of the sinking of ships, but I think in recent weeks the policy of that government has become a little more rigid in that regard, and a great many of the reports that we see in the newspapers here of shipping losses by the United States originate, I think, in the press and news agencies of that country.
My hon. friend says that Britain announces losses. In due course they do; I agree. But the time of these announcements may vary. The loss of the Prince oj Wales and the Repulse was announced almost immediately because ships of that type, of course, are easily recognizable by the enemy and the information was already in their hands. Whenever we are sure that they have a certain amount of information and the actual facts,
Postal Service

there is no reason why we should withhold the news, but until we are certain of that we might help the enemy by giving out the information.
My hon. friend says that sinkings in the St. Lawrence estuary are on a similar basis to sinkings in the Mediterranean or in the far east. I cannot agree. There are reasons which I could disclose in private to my hon. friend, but which I do not think I should make public, why sinkings in an area like the gulf of St. Lawrence or the estuary of the river St. Lawrence are in a very different position from sinkings, say, on the high seas.
I do not think I should say any more. I have discussed the matter with the intelligence branch of the Department of Naval Services. I discussed it again with them this morning, and I had the great benefit of having present at the conference this morning a member of the intelligence staff of the British Admiralty, who is now in this country. He agrees entirely as to the great necessity for very careful tensorship of any news regarding TJ-boat sinkings, and the reasons he gave and the reasons the members of my own staff gave appeal to me very strongly. Consequently I feel that at this time it would be unwise to make any further statements regarding sinkings in the St. Lawrence.

subtopic: DISTURBANCE AT VANCOUVER IMMIGRATION
speechtext:
I desire to ask certain questions
of the Minister of Labour, based on a dispatch which appeared in the Ottawa morning Journal of to-day, under date Vancouver, May 13: Army guards with fixed bayonets to-night patrolled the railway tracks in front of Vancouver's immigration building where Japanese, awaiting removal to the interior, earlier staged their first outbreak of violence since war came to the Pacific.
Late to-day, the Japanese housed in the waterfront building smashed windows, pushed an iron grating to the street and turned a fire hose upon a guard and into the street where crowds gathered.
The outbreak, described by Austin C. Taylor, chairman of the British Columbia Security Commission, as "more playful than anything else" was quickly quelled.
To-night, however, there was more unintelligible shouting and rolls of paper unfolded from the second and third storeys, Japanese faces peered from smashed windows.
Mr. Taylor said the trouble apparently resulted from refusal to allow the Japanese to converse daily with friends outside. Until to-day, Japanese women had been allowed to stand at a distance and talk to the men through the iron-grated windows. The commission chairman added that the Japanese would be removed from the building soon to road camps in the interior of the province.
"There was nothing malicious about the trouble", said Mr. Taylor, whose commission has evacuated hundreds of Japanese from the vital Pacific coast defence zones. "It was more playful than anything else. Some of the Japanese just got a little fed up about being kept in the building and got a little exuberant. There was more yelling than anything else." Scores of passers-by were attracted to the building by the shouts that accompanied the smashing of glass. Guards on a nearby viaduct

Japanese Nationals
kept onlookers at a distance as the Japanese turned a firehose out through one of the broken windows, directing the stream of water to the ground.
Although this was the first outbreak of violence, Japanese housed at Hastings park "manning depot" prior to being sent to road jobs in the interior, previously staged what they termed a "sit-down strike". They protested against the breakfasts at the local park where several thousand Japanese are housed. The following morning they ate their food and all was quiet.
Evacuation of the more than 23,000 Japanese men, women and children in British Columbia was ordered by the dominion government last January. Shortly afterwards, the B.C. Security Commission was formed to handle the evacuation and since then hundreds of Japanese have been rounded up and sent away from the coast. Some have gone to the interior and to other provinces.
My questions are: (1) what action does the government intend taking in connection with this outbreak; (2) will steps be taken to guard against any further disturbances, (3) has the present security commission any intention of removing the Japanese east of the Cascades or is it preparing a permanent camp at Hastings park, Vancouver?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: DISTURBANCE AT VANCOUVER IMMIGRATION

The camp at Hastings park is not permanent and is simply a clearing depot. Serious emergency exists in High River owing to river in flood changing its course, flooding main business section permanently. Original federal dyke holding. This needs extending. Disastrous condition needs your immediate attention.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I am not going to take up much time to-day as the minister is busy. I wish to praise a few officers of his department, especially Squadron Leader Stewart, Mr. Malcom McLean, one of our former colleagues, and also his secretary Mr. Sharpe and Miss Gough, who is an admirable private secretary. They help us at times in connection with the transfer of French-speaking men in the air force when they are isolated among people who do not speak their tongue. I wish to give credit to them for what they do in that regard.
There are two things I want to say to-day and I shall be brief. I have before me a headline in the Ottawa Journal of May 12, "U-boat sinks freighter in St. Lawrence." It is a big headline across the first page of the Journal, and of course it was also a front page headline in all the papers of the country. That headline ought to have been "U-boat sunk by R.C.A.F." I do not say that to be critical of the R.CA.F. but what I complain about is that we have not sufficient defence in this country. The Germans should be
informed that whenever they have the audacity to come inland in the St. Lawrence river, so close to us, they will meet with proper defence and that they will not be allowed to go back home. That is the first thing I want to say.
The second point is that in the united nations air conference which will take place next week, the minister should have no inferiority complex towards the delegates from any part of the world, considering the work that is being done by the R.C.A.F. jointly with the Royal Air Force in England and elsewhere in the theatres of war. I hope there will be no more commitments to send any more of our own men outside of this country before the defence of this country is assured and completed.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I should like to make one or two observations in connection with the remarks of the hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald) as recorded on page 2351 of Hansard of May 12. The hon. member indicated that the people of Brantford were disturbed and inconvenienced by the movement of the aeroplanes connected with the airport and flying school located near Brantfordl, and the flashing of the rotary beacon on that air base. I am prompted to refer to the hon. member's remarks, first because of the press publicity they have received and second because those remarks to me are indicative of an attitude of a great many Canadian citizens in connection with the prosecution of this war and the seriousness of the crisis with which this country is confronted. I have the privilege of living in a town close to the largest air training base in Canada, if not in the world, and I want to tell this committee that I lie in my bed at night listening to those planes rising from that air base day and night-
(The hon. member for Edmonton East- Mrs. Casselman-in the chair):

I was saying that as I lie in my bed at night next to that airport-

speechtext:
I see
that hon. members fully recognize the import of the statement I have just made. As I listen to those planes operating day and night, winter and summer, I thank God that these young men who are offering their services and their lives for Canada are part of Canada's contribution to this war.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
And that they are
friendly planes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
And that they are friendly planes, and that the sound of changing the pitch of the propeller is not the noise of enemy bombs dropping on Canadian soil. I repeat that it seems to me the hon. member's remarks are indicative of the complacency of the Canadian people in the present serious situation. I want to compliment the Minister of National Defence for Air, who is in charge of the Royal Canadian Air Force and the air defence of Canada; but I suggest that the sooner the citizens of Canada develop a complex of hate and revenge and determination	against our
enemies who perpetrate such atrocities as those of Hong Kong and who are sinking ships and murdering innocent seamen in the gulf of St. Lawrence, the sooner we are going to get a proper grasp on the seriousness of this war and the sooner the Canadian people will be willing to sacrifice their all in connection with our participation in the struggle.
There is not only too much complacency in Canada, there is too much individual selfishness, too much of the spirit indicated by the remarks of the hon. member for Brantford City as to inconvenience and disturbance by a beacon light on a defence air post keeping people awake. We are thinking too much of self and have not enough realization of the desperate life and death struggle in which this country is engaged. Therefore I could not refrain from making this reference to the remarks of the hon. member.
In my opinion our greatest contribution to this war effort is that made by the Royal Canadian Air Force under the empire training scheme. Next to me in the town of Trenton lives a family of which one son, one of the finest types of young Canadians, who was in

the Royal Canadian Air Force, was killed the other day bombing over France and Germany. This boy gave his life to protect my home and the homes of other Canadians, and although my home is adjacent to that air base I say to my hon. friend and to every hon. member that that boy's parents thank God every night that other young Canadians have the national spirit and the guts to fly through winter and summer learning how to bomb our enemies. And I should feel myself remiss in my duty if I did not try to impress upon hon. members the necessity of taking a different point of view of this whole situation and getting away from this petty sense of inconvenience, of being disturbed in their sleep by the light of a beacon or the noise of changing pitch of a propeller. If they are kept awake they should get out of their beds and kneel down and thank God that those young Canadians are willing to give their lives for the protection of Canadian homes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, I am delighted to join with the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition in expressing the pleasure I am sure of all hon. members in seeing you for the first time in this very responsible position. We, the members of the opposition, shall be happy to see you there often; for we know that we shall get fair and impartial treatment from the chair. I am confident you will do credit not only to yourself but to the women of Canada whom you represent in this house.
I desire now to take a moment to express my admiration of the Minister of National Defence for Air for the frank way in which he has dealt with matters relating to his department in giving information to this committee, not only in the general statement he made but also in answering the many questions put to him. I was unable to be present in the house yesterday because I had to attend another meeting, but I have looked through Hansard, and I followed the proceedings the previous day, when I was here most of the time. Many of the questions I had intended to put to the minister already have been answered, so I need not take very much time this afternoon.
Right at the outset I should like to join in what has been said already by the hon. member for Peel, the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, and the hon. member who just took his seat and others, in paying tribute to the gallant^ members of the air force both in Canada and overseas, who at all times, day and night, face great dangers. As members of parliament we cannot adequately express our admiration for these

War Appropriation-Air Services
young men. The whole of western Canada has made a wonderful contribution to the air force, and within the last ten days my own district has been very severely hit. In the first place we had a military funeral, for the first time in our history. A young man who had been overseas and who had been returned to Canada fell ill in Montreal, was taken to the hospital and died. They gave him the honour of a military funeral at Wolseley; some forty members of the air force were there; the ceremony was very inspiring and gave great comfort to the mother, who is a widow with two other sons also in the air force. On Sunday last in that same town they held a memorial service for a young man who was killed while flying over France; his death was reported in the Ottawa papers of the day before yesterday. Only to-day I received word by air mail that the son of my opponent in the last election crashed and was killed yesterday while training near Yorkton. These incidents just go to illustrate that these men are in danger all the time, whether flying over France, over the Pacific or in training in Canada. I pay my tribute to the gallantry of the members of our air force.
The minister has dealt with the three branches of his department-the home war establishment, the overseas war establishment, and the commonwealth air training plan. The minister stated the number of trained men being turned out each month under this plan, and I was pleased to see that this number is 25 per cent greater than the estimate he gave last year when his department was under review. That is encouraging, and I hope it will continue. It is important that it should, because I believe the air force is going to play a very important part in the winning of this war-and we are going to win it.
The previous speaker referred to the remarks of the hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald) who outlined some of the nuisances which had to be endured in the vicinity of an airport. When the minister was asked whether there were to be any further aerodromes established in Canada, he said there were not. Well, he has his department well in hand; I believe he knows what is best, and if we are getting the necessary number of trained men, that is all right with me. But in passing I may say that the people in some parts of my own district were encouraged a year ago, by the number of survey parties in that area, particularly those looking over some of the fields already surveyed and in use by Trans-
Canada Air Lines. I can assure the minister that if it becomes necessary to establish more training centres, we will gladly put up with any inconvenience, noise or anything of the sort that may be incidental thereto. We in Wolseley are near Regina and only about sixty miles from Yorkton. We hear the drone of aeroplanes at night, but that has never caused me any particular discomfort, nor have I lost a wink of sleep as yet.
I was encouraged to hear the statement of the minister that according to his estimate there are sufficient men available to meet the requirements of the air force at least for the next six months and perhaps for the next year. I have received many letters, and have been visited by several young men, complaining that they have been examined and accepted but that sometimes they have to wait a long time before being called up. This tends to make them discouraged. I know of some young men who were very anxious to get into the air force but had to wait so long before being called up that they went into the army instead. In this connection there is one point I should like to bring to the attention of the minister, though I believe it was pretty well discussed a day or two ago. There must be a number of men in the ground crews of the air force, with good education, who could be used to advantage in the army. They are not getting ahead very quickly in the ground crews, and I think some of them are dissatisfied.
I was pleased to read what the minister had to say with respect to equalizing the pay and allowances of the members of the air force, particularly as between sergeant pilots and commissioned officers. I am sure this will make for a much better spirit on the part of these young men, because we all agree that when they are in the air, whether they are observers, gunners, pilots or anything else, they all face the same dangers and should be treated alike. This matter has been so well dealt with, however, that I need not take up further time on it.
I have just one word of complaint to offer in conclusion, with respect to some of the training centres in Saskatchewan. I have in my hand a return which I requested on February 20, with regard to the water supply at some of the air fields and training centres in my province. According to this return, contracts were let for the drilling of wells, with gravel walls, at $15 and $18 per foot; and in addition there was a contract at S2 per foot for the test hole, a small hole about two inches in diameter. Those rates were altogether out of reason. The original contract was sublet. I appreciate the fact that the minister

War Appropriation-Air Services
cannot look after every one of these things, that someone else must do it for him, but there should be some cheek. Certainly a contract of that kind was out of all reason and proportion.
I was going to deal with the question of the salvage of oil, but on looking over Hansard I find that it has been dealt with already. A question of mine dealing with this matter was passed yesterday as an order for return, and I should have the information in due course. But I do think some attention should be given to the matter of salvaging lubricating oils and so forth at these airports.
There is one other matter which perhaps the minister should take up with some other department, possibly the Department of Mines and Resources. The government should investigate the possibilities of producing gasoline from the tar sands in the northern part of Saskatchewan and Alberta. I ask the minister to keep this in mind. This war may be won or lost because of oil supplies. There is a wonderful field in that part of the country and I trust it has not been neglected. I believe there are possibilities of producing gasoline which would mean a lot, not only to this country but to the empire.
Madam Chairman, I am not going to take up any more of the time of the committee as I know the minister is anxious to get away. I want to express my appreciation of the frank manner in which he has answered our questions. I have had occasion at times to deal with his department and I have always found the officials there ready to display the same frankness the minister has displayed here. I hope other departments will take a little tip from him. If they would, it would help to establish confidence, not only on the part of members of the house but throughout the dominion generally.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, may I first of all pay a tribute to you on the occasion of your being the first lady to assume the important duties involved in the chairmanship of the committee of the whole.
I want to say just a word about the remarks of the hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald) as to the position in which his municipality has been placed. There is a municipality in my constituency which has offered the department clear title to two sections of land if they will establish an airport in the immediate vicinity. We believe that more airports should be established in southern Manitoba. We do not know why there are not more there, because our people are ready to play their part.
I should like to pay my tribute to the gallant airmen who have done so much for us

during this war. I think the record of southern Manitoba is equal to the rest of Canada in the number of young men who have enlisted in the air force. I am sorry to say that many of them have already made the supreme sacrifice. Many of these boys come from my constituency, and I know their families personally. They have offered their all, and we cannot measure the debt we owe them.
In this connection I should like to ask the minister if the courses have been accelerated or reduced, whether these men are trained in 'the same period of time as before or in a shorter period. I am referring particularly to air crew.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I would prefer not to give any answer with respect to the length of courses or their extension.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Another matter has been raised; I believe the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Gray) brought it up first, and I have had questions on the order paper about it. I have never been able to get it clear in my mind just how commissions are granted when these young men graduate. I cannot understand why one man is given a commission and another only a sergeancy. I should like to see this matter brought up at the coming conference. I believe the young men who are members of the air crew should hold the same rank; they should all be commissioned if possible.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I feel I would be somewhat remiss in my duty if I did not come to the defence of my colleague, the hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald). I think it is unfair that so much publicity has been given to certain parts of his address the other day by certain sections of the press, especially here in Ottawa. They referred only to certain parts of his speech, which seems characteristic of some of the pre3S. This is done in an effort to have people believe the things they want them to believe for certain purposes of their own. I am proud to say that our local paper, the Brantford Expositor, does not put any unfair interpretation upon the remarks of my colleague. I am very happy to say that that is probably characteristic of the people that he and I have the honour to represent. They try to face issues and facts fairly and clearly.
I read the speech of the hon. member and I could not read into his remarks any complaint from the people of Brantford. The fact of the matter is that on page 2352 of Hansard he made this statement:
The people are not complaining about having these airports in their districts, but there are two sides to the story.

War Appropriation-Air Services
It is only fair to the hon. member for Brantford City to say that he emphasized the two sides of the situation. The hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) has justed stated that he would like to have some of these airports in his constituency, and that only brings to light the desirability of this privilege. However, for every privilege we receive there is a corresponding responsibility, and the bon. member for Brantford City pointed out that the people of Brantford welcomed the opportunity of accepting the responsibility that goes with that privilege.
I feel I should refer to the remarks of the hon. member for Northumberland, Ont., (Mr. Fraser) and the hon. member for Souris. There have been no people more anxious to serve in this war effort than the people of Brant and the people of Brantford whom the hon. member and I represent in this house. The record of enlistments from this particular community will compare favourably with that of any other section of the dominion. I do not want to boast, but the fact is that in the little town of Paris in my constituency, which takes in part of the city of Brantford as well, 8 per cent of the population has enlisted. That is evidence of their desire to serve. From now on the less said about these remarks the better, but if anything is to be said I hope that mention is made of both sides of the case.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What are the two sides?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The privilege and the responsibility. The hon. member was just emphasizing that there were two sides. I might mention *that one of these military camps is situated on property which was donated to the Department of National Defence by the Six Nations Indians. .There has been little or no comment about that. There will be no taxes to be paid by the government, in fact there is no obligation whatever upon the government. This is characteristic not only of the people of the Six Nations but of the people of the city of Brantford. I might say also that the Six Nations council donated $1,000 annually to the Red Cross from their meagre funds. I ask hon. members, therefore, to familiarize themselves with some of the contributions made by the people in this district before they make any criticism of them.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Madam Chairman, there are one or two matters I should like to have the minister keep in mind when the air conference meets next week. I know he is anxious to get away and I shall be as brief as possible.
In his statement the minister made reference to his recent visit to Great Britain. As
I see it, the war situation to-day has changed since then and since the battles in the far east; we have lost the command of the sea in the Pacific, and I would ask the minister bo bear that in mind at the air conference next week. I believe that that conference will be the forerunner of what Australia has been asking for from the British authorities for six months, namely, a -war cabinet on which Britain and the dominions will be represented, as there was in the last war, for quick and united empire action. The situation so far as Australia, New Zealand and South Africa are concerned has changed greatly through Japanese command of sea power in the Pacific and the way Japan is roaming around there. These three dominions are in grave danger. Mr. Curtin has spoken very strongly of the need of Australian representation where empire policy is being discussed, and Mr. Menzies, the former prime minister, also referred to it in this chamber and since. Those two very able prime ministers of Australia pointed out that empire policy decisions with respect to the war, and affecting all these dominions, were being made in the far east and other theatres when they were not present, decisions which went against them, and that they were not consulted on what empire policy should be. I think that is shown by the loss of our supremacy of the sea in the Pacific and by the battles in the far east. In the last war the empire war cabinet was a great success. Each dominion prime minister or his nominee was a member. It saved the war from being lost. I hope the minister will bear this in mind and not press too strongly for anything different at the air conference next week or for Canada to act separately from the other dominions.
We are all proud of what Canada has done so far in the air. It makes a glorious page in the history of the empire, but I hope that the minister at that conference will listen to Australia and New Zealand and the mother country because I believe that the most important matter to be decided at the conference is whether or not the dominions are to have a say in empire policy in the far east, in the Pacific and on the Atlantic and other theatres of war-to act together to save the empire-and of course air power is intimately related to the command of the sea, as well as command of the land. Australia and New Zealand, after the losses in the far east, made a strong appeal to the United States for help, and they are getting it. Canada should qualify for aid on the same status also, for its empire training scheme.
The defence policy of this country has two cardinal points: one is home defence, and the other is to protect Canada's neutrality in case

War Appropriation-Air Services
the American continent is attacked by a foreign power, meaning Japan; and Japan has already made that attack at Pearl Harbour, an attack which shocked the civilized world. In my opinion, if Australia and New Zealand can get aid under the lease-lend or other bills of the United States, and aid as allies, and they are getting it, so should Canada; for this country has helped the united nations war effort by building advanced air bases on both oceans and by the empire air training scheme. If any country is entitled to qualify for aid under the lease-lend and other aid bills it is Canada, and I hope that these matters will be remembered at the air conference next week.
I trust that something will also be done to rectify the inequalities of pay in the air force, which are very serious. Some civilian members of the air force are in uniform as pilot officers-a misnomer

and receive higher pay than pilots, sergeants, gunners and observers who are flying over Germany. I think the minister himself, who is a good business administrator, will agree with me that changes should be made in that respect immediately and these inequalities removed.
I should also like to see a change made in the syllabus and schedule of training at the manning pool in Toronto. In the last war the men remained at the manning pool for only two or three days, but in this war some of them have been there for weeks and months, some of them from last September, and for over a year have had only guard duty and infantry drill. Perhaps the minister has given some explanation of this, but I know that it is very unsatisfactory to the men, many of whom gave up good positions expecting to get overseas at an early date, to have to stay at the manning pool doing precision drills, infantry drill, marching up the Humber and back, and doing guard duty. It is far too much for them; it is a waste of time where training is costly and should be speeded up.
As I said when the Minister of Munitions and Supply introduced his first bill in connection with the Trans-Canada Air Lines, I wanted him to take over the pioneers, the civilian clubs. I appreciate what the civilian flying clubs did before the war. I said in the last parliament, when I was sitting where the hon. member for Lake Centre now sits, that the civilian flying clubs did great work before the war in giving flying instruction and in educating the people to become air-minded at a time when Canada was sleeping. I think these schools should be united now in an empire air training scheme with the two great railway systems of this country, because civil aviation after the war is going to be the greatest thing in the world, particularly in Canada. That is IMr. Church.]
one of the great issues in England to-day, and the air minister for Great Britain made a statement about it after there had been a prolonged debate in parliament. I hope the minister will bear these matters in mind at the air conference next week.

I should like to refer
to a question I had on the order paper for a couple of weeks and which was answered yesterday by the Minister of National Defence for Air. My question had reference to the deputy minister of national defence for air. I will read the question and the answer and then point out what I believe to be a wrong condition of affairs.
My question consisted of five parts. Question 1 was:
Is S. L. de Carteret, deputy minister of National Defence for Air?
The answer to that was "yes." Question 2 was:
If so, (a) when was he appointed, (b) what is his present salary?
The answer to that was:
(a) February 1, 1941;	(b) no salary or
allowance from the government.
Question 3 was:
What was his business, trade or profession before accepting his present position with the government ?
The answer to that was:
Mr. S. L. de Carteret, vice president and general manager, Canadian International Paper Company; president, Continental Paper Products Limited; president, Masonite Company of Canada Limited; president, International Fibre Board Limited.
Question 4 was:
Does he continue active connection with his former business, trade or profession while in the employ of the government?
The answer to that was "yes." Question 5 was:

I think it is wrong policy to have what is generally termed a dollar-a-year man in the position of deputy' minister of a department as important as the Department of National Defence for Air. This department is important enough to have a deputy minister who would be free to give his full time to the work of the department, without being distracted in any way by business concerns of his own. It

should be a matter of policy for the government that no business man shall be put in an important civil service position and continue at the same time to attend to his own businesses. I do not know whether the minister knows it or not, but there are two things which I should like to tell him. First, the people of Canada generally are very much disturbed about the influence of big business in the government.
The people of Canada have not forgotten the exposure of big business methods made by a special committee of this house which was later appointed as a royal commission, in 1934; I refer to the price spreads and mass buying committee and commission. Secondly, I tell the minister that the present government of Canada, despite professions it may make to the country, has an exceedingly bad name with organized labour. Organized labour is convinced that the hostile labour policy of the government is influenced by these big business men who have unlimited access to the government. I could name quite a number of them-men I have known over the years-who have opposed consistently every attempt by the workers to better their condition and every item of social legislation which was brought forward in either this parliament or any of the legislatures of the provinces.
With regard to the deputy minister of the Department of National Defence for Air, it has been brought to my attention that the employees affiliated with one of the Canadian congresses have been negotiating with Continental Paper Products Limited since November, 1941. The agreement has been before Mr. de Carteret since early in March of this year, and they cannot get any action on their negotiations because he says he has not time to deal with the matter.' The Department of Labour advise this organization that they are quite powerless to compel Mr. de Carteret or anyone else to negotiate with or recognize labour organizations. What I want to point out is, that this government has gone on record as favouring the principle of collective bargaining; it passed an order in council to that effect and gave it a great deal of publicity, but that order in council has not only been ignored by the heads of industry generally throughout the dominion but has been particularly and flagrantly ignored by business men in high positions in the government, or if you like, in the civil service. Therefore I think we have a right to insist that deputy ministers in charge of departments such as the one under the Deputy Minister of National Defence for Air should be civil servants, without any outside business ties or
obligations. There is no doubt that a person qualified to do that work can be found, and 1 insist that we adopt that principle and see that the government is not influenced by persons who are acting directly contrary to the very principles for which we are fighting.

I wish to bring to the attention of the minister and the committee certain information tabled on May 13 when I received answers to the following questions as recorded at page 2385 of Hansard:
1. On what date was the National Steel Car Corporation at Malton authorized to proceed with the production of Martin bombers?
The answer was "April 26, 1941." My second question was:

The answer was: "Canadian government authorities." I presume, from the answer the minister gave to a question I asked two days ago, that that contract would be authorized or requisitioned from his department. The third question was:

To which the answer was given:
Advance notice of cancellation was given on November 26, 1941.
I call attention to the fact that that was eight months after the project was authorized. The answer continues:
Final cancellation was given on December 29, 1941.
A full nine months after the beginning of the undertaking.
The next question was:

I am surprised at the answer to this question, in view of the assurance given us by the Minister of National War Services some days ago that the committee investigating war expenditures last year was satisfied with the checks provided in this matter. The answer is:

-although that was completed five months ago-

My own information from the plant is that as many as 500 or 600 men were engaged on that project for the eight or nine months. The fifth question was:

The answer is:

The answer was none. The next question was "Why was the project abandoned?" And the answer:

That is eight or nine months after the project had been under way.
-that a very substantial amount of reengineering had to be done before the plan would be satisfactory-involving perhaps six months' delay.
In view of the fact that the British government was pressing for another type of bomber and that this particular type could be obtained in the United States in less time than it took to produce it in Canada, the plan was changed.
I think the people of this country are entitled to know why it required eight or nine months to discover that a certain process of reengineering was required on this project, after well over three-quarters of a million dollars had been spent. Here you had hundreds of men working and this expenditure made at a time when the planes were needed. The minister should give the committee some further explanation. Nothing caused more distrust in the vicinity of greater Toronto of the ability of the government to produce in our factories the things needed in our war effort than the outcome of this experiment. These workers were all working in the greater Toronto area, and everyone was asking: Why is it that the government has to engage hundreds of men for eight or nine months on a project and then abandon it? Engineers of the plant told me that these jigs were absolutely valueless for the production of any other plane. Would the minister enlighten us on this subject?
