Mr. Chairman, since I last reported to the house on the work of the Department of Munitions and Supply, the nature of our problems has changed considerably. I may say that up to the present time the department has placed contracts totalling in excess of $4,000,000,000, which is a sum considerably larger than the national debt of Canada prior to the outbreak of war. Our programme is by no means frozen, as is evidenced by the fact that capital assistance granted in the month of April exceeded $25,000,000. Capital assistance granted up to the present time amounts to about $380,000,000, or slightly less than 10 per cent of the total orders for munitions placed by the department.
The last time I reported, the majority of our plants were still in the process of tooling up and expanding production. To-day by far the greater part are fully tooled and staffed, and are producing at something like the maximum rate. We have had some very satisfactory results from these plants. In nearly

every case we have found that the output considerably exceeds the objective for which the plant was built. Our explosive plants are, I think, producing something like 75 per cent over the estimated plant capacity. There has been some balancing up carried on, but it has been possible to step up the production of these plants to this extent. One gun plant is producing two and a half times the guns that we anticipated it would produce, or that we provided machinery for. In general, our preliminary estimates of production have been found to be conservative, and we have very little to apologize for in that connection.
Another satisfactory feature of the programme is the cost of our products, because costs are a sure index of efficiency. We find that where a plant is in full or nearly full production, the cost of our product compares favourably with the cost either in the United States or in the United Kingdom. We find also that our quality has been all that can be desired. Frequently I have been told officially that the ammunition we sent to England, both small arms and artillery, is placed in the preferred category and is eagerly sought after. We used to mark our small arms ammunition "suitable for use by air force," but we received objections from the other services that the air force was being given preference with our ammunition. We now label it without reference to the air force in order that all three services may share in it.
I might run briefly over the operations of the department and perhaps prepare the way for any questions that hon. members may desire to ask. In the matter of production, speaking generally with reference to the criticisms that have been made in this house of management holding back production or of inefficient management, I think the executives of my department can now stream-line a plant as well as any executives in Canada. We can show you, Mr. Chairman, some of the finest organizations to be found anywhere, plants of which any manufacturer would be proud. But I must say that it is impossible to stream-line a plant and plan work for the various units while the plant is expanding rapidly.
As an example of this, I would point out that the aeroplane industry has expanded its personnel forty times since the war began. The average intake of new men into this industry exceeds 2,000 a month. These men come from the farms and the schools without any mechanical training, and it is necessary to teach them to do the work they will ultimately perform. For that reason, any one going through an aeroplane factory often sees men standing around who seem to be idle. The fact is that they are studying the work

War Appropriation-Supplies
of the men. in front of them; they are, in fact, learners. We also have men who say that they could turn out more work, but we find that we must insist on less speed and more care at the start. I recall one very bright man who went into an aeroplane plant full of zeal and ambition but with absolutely no mechanical knowledge. The foreman stayed over him the first day to teach him one particular process, but on the second day he was placed on his own. He decided that he would show the foreman what he could do. He turned out a tremendous amount of work, but it was found that he had destroyed over $3,000 worth of stock and had produced nothing which would be useful in an aeroplane.
I could cite a number of examples of the difficulty of organizing a plant while it is being started up or where it is subject to rapid expansion. If any hon. members go through a new plant and hear stories of that kind, I hope they will assess the full picture. I hope they will ask: "Is it a plant being expanded, or is it a plant that is up to capacity and should be running efficiently?" When hon. members hear stories of men wrho can do more work, I hope my hon. friends will take that into account.
The same thing, of course, applies to plants that are retooling. It is an obvious sequence of war that the type of weapons changes from time to time. A shell that is needed to-day may not be needed to-morrow. If that is the case there is only one thing to do, tear down your tooling and tool for the type of shell that is required. The type of air fighting changes, and it is necessary to change the type of aeroplane or perhaps introduce modifications on the type being built.
We go out of the production of domestic motor cars, and it is necessary to stop production lines to change the tooling and accept a loss of time, even amounting to several months, before the production line can be turned over to the new product. Everyone who has been associated with the motor car industry is well aware of this situation. Ever since motor cars have been built by mass production, the industry has expected a lay-off of from two to three months in the summer while the production lines are being changed for the new models. The production of a new model is started over a year in advance of the first car being produced. That is incidental to mass production. It is not a situation confined to motor cars. It is true of almost every article that depends upon mass production for its output.
Just to run over the progress in the various fields, as hon. members will appreciate, our shipbuilding industry is still expanding rapidly.
We have perhaps two yards in Canada that are fully manned; the other seventeen yards are still in progress of expansion. One new large six-berth yard in Montreal laid down its first keels last week. At the present time we are launching a 10,000-ton merchant ship every four days, and we expect later on to bring this period down to three days. The yards of the great lakes and some of the yards on deep water are full-out in the production of corvettes and mine-sweepers. Those yards are still being expanded; new berths are being built, and that type of construction is getting near the objective as far as output is concerned. In the small boat field I think we have built some 14,000 small boats since the war began, and this field is fairly active, particularly in connection with the wooden Fairmile, the wooden minesweeper and smaller craft.
In the matter of aircraft, our production is now stepped up to about 400 planes a month, and we have plants that are not in production. A large plant on the west coast that is building PBY boats is just coming into production. I believe the first plane is being test-flown at about this time. We have three other plants which are working on new types of planes and which will not be in production for some months. The plants that have been standardized on certain models and given unlimited production are beginning to step up their production to very satisfactory proportions. I may say that at the commencement the aeroplane industry was quite small, and orders for our own air force were small. The industry was then dealing direct with England and taking small orders from there. We had orders of fifty, one hundred and two hundred planes in process, and many changes in tooling were necessary. We have now reduced our production to nine types of planes, and the plants are cleaning up old orders and concentrating on one type of production for each plant with accordingly improved results. At the present time we are looking after all the requirements of the air training plan. We are building operational planes for our own air force, and we have accepted substantial orders for operational training planes from England and from the United States.
I should like to speak particularly of Federal Aircraft company. That company has been criticized severely in this house, and recently a number of newspaper and other articles have appeared reflecting on its work. I think the work of this company is more outstanding than any other item of aircraft production. The reason for starting the company, as hon. gentlemen will remember, is that at the time of Dunkirk, we suddenly received notice that

War Appropriation-Supplies
the promised Anson planes for our air training programme could no longer be sent from England. The company was formed in July, 1940. It had no plant. All the plants at that time were loaded with orders up to their then very small capacity, and the company was told to go out on the highways and byways and find manufacturing capacity for the planes it was to build.
The company had also a big redesigning job on hand. The Anson plane was suitable for English production and designed to English standards, and it was impossible to break that plane down and have it built to English standards in the small shops of Canada. While this redesigning job was going on, numerous changes were made in the plane. Originally it had a fixed undercarriage, but the design was changed and a retractable undercarriage put in. A new type of motor was also put in the plane, and numerous other changes were made in the fittings to make the plane suitable for Canadian training requirements. That redesigning job was carried through, and the first plane was ready for flight in June, 1941. Production of the Anson has reached well over 600 planes. We planned for a certainly monthly production, and I may say that the actual production has run SO per cent over the planned production and could be speeded up more than that. We have not only filled the requirements of the Canadian air force but have accepted orders from purchasers elsewhere, and we expect that the industry which has been established by Federal Aircraft, which carries some fifty or sixty plants in all parts of Canada, will be a continuing industry for a very considerable time.
Does the minister mean after the war?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
No, but certainly until the end of the war.
In automotive vehicles the industry is going full-out. Over a quarter of a million vehicles have been produced and shipped abroad. I think our vehicles have been in every area of active combat. The most interesting of all the vehicles is the universal carrier. Its production has been stepped up to a very large output indeed, many times the output that was first contemplated.
In tanks, the Angus shops are running at a very uniform pace, meeting the objective that was set for that company. No week goes by, I think, when the required number of tanks is not produced. We made certain commitments on tanks and other equipment for Russia, and at the end of the first three months we were exactly even with our commitments,

having shipped on the due date every tank and every piece of equipment that had been promised.
Our other tank arsenal, which is the second largest tank arsenal on this continent, is not up to capacity. There has been delay in obtaining delivery of transmissions. That has been the main difficulty. The output of transmissions for all tanks on this continent was organized in the United States, but the manufacturers have not lived up to promises, with the result that for the last several months every transmission as it is received can be put into a tank and the tank driven away at once. If a transmission comes into the factory in the morning, it goes into a tank, which is driven out of the factory the same afternoon. All the problems connected with the design and production of tanks have been solved, and to-day it is just a matter of assembling the necessary material to bring our big tank arsenal up to its objective.
Any production of engines in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: No; the engines are not made in this country.
Transmissions?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
Nor transmissions, except
the infantry tank transmissions. They are made in this country. The Ram transmissions are not.
In the production of naval guns great progress has been made. We are making quite a list of naval guns. I think all of them are in substantial production, except a factory in Vancouver which is just getting into production.
We have had particularly good results with the production of gun mountings and the fittings that go with the gun, which are more of a mechanical problem than the gun itself. In every case our gun-mounting programme is ahead of the manufacture of the guns themselves.
We have also carried out a very considerable programme, for both our own navy and the British navy, of producing special radio equipment and accessories such as firing mechanisms for naval ships.
In the matter of field guns and small arms our programme is almost completely in production. We have one plant at Windsor making automatic guns for tanks, which is not yet in production. We intended that plant for a different type of production, but due to changing requirements overseas we had to retool, which has rather set back production. But that plant will be the last of

War Appropriation-Supplies
our big automatic gun plants to go into production. The Inglis plant-we have expanded that again and again, and any figures I have given in the past about the production of the Bren gun, the Colt-Browning and the Boys anti-tank gun, have been greatly exceeded. Unfortunately I cannot give actual production figures because I have agreed that we shall not give even approximate figures for this type of production.
The government arsenal making rifles-Lee-Enfields-and Sten guns is getting up to capacity. It is not at capacity with respect to rifles but is stepping up at the present time at the rate of 4,000 rifles a month, and we hope to get capacity by August. In the matter of Sten guns the production is very large indeed, and is stepping up by a thousand or more each month.
As regards field artillery, the 25-pounder guns are being produced at more than fifty per cent over the rated capacity of the plant. The 3-7 anti-aircraft guns are coming into production. A substantial number of guns and mounts were shipped last month as complete and tested, and it is expected that the output will step up by geometrical progression as we go on. That is the largest and most complicated gun that we have undertaken, and the bringing of it into substantial production is a major feat of our gun programme.
The Bofors gun programme, which was delayed because of production troubles, is now swinging along very well. The one hundredth gun was produced last month; the number will be very substantially increased this month, and we expect to bring that plant up to full production about September. All present needs- certainly all needs in Canada-have been supplied, and we are now taking care of export requirements.
In the tank and anti-tank gun field, as I mentioned before, output has greatly exceeded our plans, and we are in a most comfortable position in both those supplies. We are making a very large number of bomb-throwers, several sizes, rocket-guns, and almost everything in that line, and all in very substantial quantities.
In the matter of ammunition we have forty plants at present turning out artillery ammunition, and it is being produced at the rate of millions a month. Types have changed frequently, which caused interruptions, but in general the production is well over the planned capacity.
We are also turning out aerial bombs, trench-mortar bombs and anti-tank mines in very considerable quantities.
The chemicals and explosives branch is still being expanded as requisitions for new explosives and new chemicals come to us. This has been a most satisfactory branch of the work of the department. As I said some time ago, many of our explosive plants-I believe practically all of them-are producing some 75 per cent over the original planned capacity. Our chemicals are being expanded to keep up with the increased rate of production, and we are really turning out ammunition-sufficient to do all our own shell-filling, of both small arms ammunition and artillery ammunition-and bombs, and we have a very large surplus which is shipped to the United Kingdom.
In the matter of small arms ammunition we are getting up over a billion rounds per annum. Our own arsenals, and government plants under private management have all come into production in a very satisfactory way. We are still expanding very largely in the small arms ammunition field. It seems to be one field in which Canada excels all countries. We have been pressed continually for more production and a wider variety of production. We are taking on new lines as rapidly as we can absorb them, and I think we can say that the expansion of that type of production will go on for a considerable time.
The industry and subcontract coordination branch is making steady progress. This is a most helpful branch of our department in the present situation. It is making a specialty of helping displaced industries, and remarkable results have been accomplished. I will 'not say for a minute that the branch is able to take care of all displaced industries. Many peace-time industries are not equipped to do useful war work, and these cases present a real problem. But the industry and subcontract coordination branch have done much to help to fill up the small machine-shop, and a great deal to put war work into displaced peace-time industrial plants.
The construction division is extremely active. I believe that both in the field of buildings and in that of airport construction the year 1942 will be the largest building season we have had. Each season we think the next season will see a slackening off, but the needs of our air training plan for operational airports, and for new training centres for both the military and the air force, seem to pyramid rather than to decline.
The wartime industries control board is a matter of great interest at the present time. I will follow my notes in discussing the work of that board.
War Appropriation-Supplies

The intensification of the war has reemphasized the importance of the part played by the system of economic controls centralized and coordinated by the wartime industries control board. Within the Department of Munitions and Supply there are twelve controllers, whose duties are to ensure that the materials or services within their respective productions are forthcoming for war needs in adequate quantities. Each of these controllers is therefore endowed with wide powers appropriate to his particular function. Each controller, broadly speaking, exercises powers to do two things: first, to see that the necessary productive facilities are expanded as far as possible; second, to limit and, where necessary, to prohibit production for civilian use in the case of those materials which are scarce in relation to war and essential demands.
I might say that the difference between the industries control board in my department and the wartime prices and trade board in the Department of Finance is that my controllers interest themselves only in materials and supplies which are urgently required for war, whereas the other board deals with peacetime commodities.
It will be readily realized, however, that if the difficult and complex task of diverting production away from civilian toward war use is to be accomplished in an effective, orderly manner and without unnecessary dislocation, a high degree of coordination of policy and procedure is necessary. The necessity of such coordination and control is the more apparent now that we have reached the stage that restrictions on production for civilian purposes must in many instances be severe, and when in some cases outright prohibitions are necessary.
Accordingly, since its reconstitution in August, 1941, the wartime industries control board has existed to promote coordination and integration of the functions of the twelve controllers and also to provide a centralized point of contact between the control agencies of this department and other governmental agencies dealing with related problems.
The board is structurally designed to facilitate such coordination. It is composed of the chairman, who is also the director-general of the priorities branch of the Department of Munitions and Supply, and twelve controllers; the chairman of the wartime prices and trade board and the president of the commodity prices stabilization corporation.
No order of an individual controller having general application is valid until it receives the consideration and signed approval of the chairman of the board, and if the order involves the imposition of a production quota

the minister's signature is also required. Any order involving price fixing requires in addition the signed concurrence of the chairman of the wartime prices and trade board.
The board holds regular meetings for the formulation of control policy and for the consideration of problems of individual controllers in relation thereto. In addition, an opportunity for day-to-day discussion and exchange of information is provided through the office of the chairman and through the board's secretariat. Liaison with the wartime prices and trade board is particularly close since the chairman of each board sits as a member of the other board and because action by controllers with respect to price requires the concurrence of the wartime prices and trade board.
Recently, with a view to avoiding duplication of administrative machinery, a working arrangement has been concluded whereby wartime industries control board controllers have agreed to extend their spheres of interest and to perform additional duties as administrators for the wartime prices and trade board. Also, with a view to avoiding duplication, the wartime prices and trade board has made available to the wartime industries control board the use of its regional office facilities and its investigatory and policing organizations.
As custodians of materials required for the war programme, the wartime industries control board is directly interested in the matter of exports. Accordingly, the chairman of the board as well as the metals controller sit as members of the advisory committee on export control, and the board is also directly represented on the executive subcommittee of that body. In like manner the board has direct representation on the shipping priorities committee, which committee is concerned with the provision of shipping space for the importation of essential materials into Canada. Contact with other governmental agencies is maintained on a less formal basis, but is nonetheless effective. In addition, the board may and does make recommendations to its minister from time to time with regard to specific problems as they may arise.
I do not propose to review all the individual orders issued by the controllers and approved by the chairman of the board since the board's inception. There have been over 100 of them. It may, however, be of interest, as an indication of the manner in which the board is dealing with the problems that confront it, if I review briefly the high lights of recent actions taken primarily as a result of the conditions created by the extension of the war into the Pacific.

War Appropriation-Supplies
Immediately upon the outbreak of hostilities in this new theatre of war, the board met with a view to effecting such additional control measures as appeared necessary by reason of the threat to our Pacific supply lines. Immediate action was, of course, taken to conserve vital supplies of rubber. As an initial temporary measure an order was issued by the controller of supplies freezing dealers' stocks of tires and tubes and suspending the processing of raw rubber generally for other than defence or munitions projects. Acting concurrently, the motor vehicle controller prohibited the supplying of spare tires and tubes as motor vehicle equipment. Subsequently the processing of rubber has been permitted for the time being only in the case of an extremely restricted list of clearly essential uses. The use of crude rubber for civilian purposes has been so restricted that the volume so conserved has been reduced by over 70 per cent in the past two months. I may say that very much less than 30 per cent is being used for civilian purposes at the present time.
The manufacture of tires for passenger automobiles was discontinued on December 12 last. The sale of new tires and tubes to the general public has been prohibited completely and may be made only in the case of a very much restricted eligible list of essential public services, and only then under permit and on delivery by the purchaser of a used tire or tube, as the case may be, for which no allowance or payment may be made.	-
Supplies of used tubes and tires have also been brought under control by establishing appropriate restrictions and requirements of proof of necessity.
While on the subject of rubber, I should mention two noteworthy developments on the supply side. With the cooperation of the wartime industries control board, arrangements have been made for the establishment of a governmental corporation known as Tolymer corporation to produce synthetic rubber in Canada. Work is under way on the preliminary plans and specifications, and it is expected that production will begin before the end of 1943. When the plants are working at capacity, the output will approximate 27,000 tons a year.
I should be careful to point out that this synthetic production will in no way relieve the civilian shortage, since every last ounce of the synthetic product will be earmarked for war purposes.
We have also set up a scrap rubber division of the Department of Munitions and Supply, which will devote its entire time to the collection of scrap rubber throughout Canada.
Arrangements have been made for the government to absorb freight charges in connection with collection so that the price paid for scrap rubber will be the same in all parts of Canada. The scrap rubber so acquired will be used for the manufacture of reclaimed rubber which, in turn, will be employed in the manufacture of war materials and vitally necessary civilian articles.
The automotive industry normally consumes large quantities of steel, rubber and oil, as well as other essential materials. Hence production of passenger automobiles for civilian use has ceased completed as of April 1. This has meant that the total number of passenger cars produced in Canada in 1942 for civilian use will be approximately 7,900 units compared with approximately 81,700 units in 1941 and 94,633 in 1940. Out of the automobiles completed from parts already fabricated, the motor vehicle controller is establishing a bank or reserve supply of some 4,000 cars to be drawn upon only for essential use as occasion may arise in future. As from March 14 the production of motor trucks for other than defence and munitions purposes has been prohibited except under permit from the motor vehicle controller. The transit controller has also issued an order banning the operation of buses for sightseeing tours and prohibiting all charter trips of a non-essential nature except those which may be directly identified with the war programme.
With regard to gasoline, it is, I think, fortunate that the basis of a civilian rationing programme had been established prior to the extension of the war into the Pacific and the recent serious increase in tanker sinkings along the Atlantic seaboard. Organizational work in connection with the rationing plan has now been satisfactorily completed and, as hon. members know, rationing was effective as from April 1. I may say that the results to date indicate a reduction of about 40 per cent in the gasoline which we expected to have consumed in that month without rationing, which, I think, is a fairly satisfactory reduction.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Forty per cent less than the minister expected would be consumed?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
Yes. In comparing it with
the month previous there must be taken into account the fact that in the months of January, February and March there was a substantial increase in use over that of the corre.-sponding months of last year. The actual decrease in April of this year compared with April of last year is 34 per cent, but taking

War Appropriation-Supplies
account of the normal increase as indicated by the first three months I think the reduction is estimated at about 43 per cent.
That is civilian?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Yes.
Not the army?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
No. That reduction is, I
think, due largely to people being careful about the manner in which they use gasoline rather than to the size of the unit, which at the moment is a fairly generous allowance.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
There is
another factor:	many people have not
obtained licences for all the cars they have.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
In other words people are
conscious of the fact that gasoline is scarce, and they are being careful.

What is the increase
in the first three months of this year as compared with the corresponding months of last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
I think it is about 12 per
cent.

Is there any special
reason for that?
Mr. HOWE.:	No; just greater business
activity.
Would the minister explain the shortage of gasoline?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
My hon. friend asked me if
that was pleasure driving or commercial. As far as civilian use is concerned it is both. It does not apply to the military, but gasoline for both commercial andl pleasure purposes must be bought through authorized pumps, and it is to consumption from those pumps that I am referring.
That 40 per cent saving would not take care of the air force?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
No; the air force requirements are growing, as are those of the military. That is not under the control of this department.
Hon. members are, of course, aware that there is no shortage of petroleum in the western hemisphere; the matter is wholly one of transportation. Therefore the position varies in different parts of Canada. The prairies are largely self-sufficient through the produc- [DOT] tion of the Turner valley and' importations from adjoining states. That situation is quite stable. On the Pacific coast we had a serious situation. We diverted part of our

tanker capacity so that we could look after that coast with our own tankers. There has been no serious inconvenience through losses of ships on that coast, and the position of the Pacific coast can now be said to be normal.
The position in Ontario, particularly southern Ontario, depends on a pipeline from the midwest field, and the usual supplies have been coming in by that pipeline. The pipeline has been operated to full capacity every moment for at least a year, and it is still operating at capacity. Where we are finding great difficulty is on the Atlantic seaboard and in Quebec, which is supplied from the Atlantic seaboard.
How long is the pipeline that brings in the oil from across the line?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Into Ontario. It comes from Oklahoma. I do not know the mileage. It is fed from the Oklahoma and midwest field.

It comes to Sarnia, does
it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Yes. All of us who read the papers appreciate that the sinking of tankers on the Atlantic has been a very serious matter. Also the loss of certain oil fields in the far east has made necessary the diversion of tankers on voyages from that area. The result is there is a serious shortage of tankers. The situation for the maritime provinces, Quebec and eastern Ontario is far from satisfactory. The needs of the army, navy and air force are reasonably protected, but civilian use is running on an extremely thin margin.

In view of the shortage of oil and gasoline in the maritimes has the department taken any steps to investigate the possibility of developing very large oil shales in different parts of Nova Scotia; Pictou, Antigonish and other counties and on Cape Breton island; also Albert county in New Brunswick where there is a very big shale field?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: I am attempting to make a statement. Would my hon. friend be kind enough to ask me that later? I can hardly keep to the thread of my discussion and answer questions of that kind at the same time.
The minister should be allowed to complete his statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
The purpose of rationing is to have the gasoline situation under control, as far as the commercial and domestic field is concerned, and to be able to divide equitably among the users such gasoline as we have. I wish those who speculate about the future of the gasoline ration would keep that in mind. When it is necessary, in order to divide fairly

War Appropriation-Supplies
such gasoline as we can obtain, to reduce the amount deliverable on a coupon that will be done, but it is very bad for the morale of the people for the newspapers to be constantly forecasting cuts which are not under contemplation. When a cut in the amount issued on gasoline ration tickets is necessary it will be made immediately. There will be no forecasting; before anyone can have time to forecast what will happen to-morrow, the thing will be done. Therefore I hope that there will be less speculation about the future of the gasoline coupon. Its purpose is to divide the available gasoline fairly, and it will be used for that purpose.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There has been a cut already, has there not?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Then the
newspapers are wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Quite. The newspapers have forecast cuts in gasoline coupons many times, but there has been no cut. When there is a out it will be because there is not enough gasoline to go round, and by cutting the amount deliverable on a coupon we shall spread more fairly what is available.
Have not the B category books been called in?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: No, but there have been certain reclassifications. In the issue of coupon books we had to scratch an organization together in short order. We called for the help of the provinces. It was cheerfully given and an attempt was made to do a good job. But the application forms for the higher categories have been reviewed to see whether the necessity was real, and we found that many people had obtained needlessly high categories. In these cases the books are being called in and proper categories issued. But that is not a change in the system; it is simply an attempt to perfect the system.

Then there is no truth
m the statement that everyone is to be placed in category A?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: No. If I were doing the thing again, I would do it in that way, because experience shows it would be a better way, and then, by another book, make special provision for those entitled to it. When we started with this system we did not foresee the zeal that people would show in order to get higher categories. When the books are issued for 1943, I think we shall have a much better system.
There should be some system of numbering.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
Yes, and better binding. But the thing was done hurriedly. We were pioneers. We deserve some credit for that. The United States are following our system and will probably improve it, but for a pioneer system it works pretty well.
Steps have also been taken to conserve further the use of essential metals. The metals controller has prohibited the sale of pig-tin for civilian use without his permission, and has drastically restricted or prohibited the use of tin and tin alloys in certain products. The controller of supplies has taken action with respect to a long list of nonessential metal products. Production of some of these articles has been prohibited entirely, while manufacture of the remainder which possess some degree of essentiality has been materially curtailed. Further curtailments have been made in the production quotas of refrigerators and washing machines, while in the case of radios production for civilian use ceased entirely after January 31, except under permit from the controller.
Also as part of a programme aimed at the conservation of essential materials, manila hemp, sisal and kapok have been brought under the jurisdiction of the controller of supplies and appropriate conservation measures effected.
Since the end of January, the powers of the controller of construction have been enlarged to give him jurisdiction over the entire construction field with the exception of equipment, plant or buildings owned or financed by the federal government. Prior to that date, the jurisdiction of the controller did not apply to one-, two- and three-family dwellings, structures erected in connection with certain primary industries, churches, public hospitals, educational institutions or buildings financed by or under the control of any provincial government, which categories were, as of January 30, brought under his control. Under his powers as revised, in the case of any building other than a plant, all projects in excess of $5,000 must be licensed by the controller before being undertaken. In such case, the cost of construction, repairs, alterations, additions and installation of equipment, if forming part of one project must be considered together as one amount in calculating the maximum value permitted without licence. In the case of a plant, equipment to the value of $5,000 may be installed without a permit, in addition to a total value of $5,000 so allowed for construction, repairs, additions and alterations. The controller has

War Appropriation-Supplies

also been given jurisdiction over production and use of construction materials and facilities.
In this as in other areas of control, the broad powers of the controller are exercised to the end that non-essential projects involving the use of scarce materials shall be postponed for the duration of the war. This basic principle of control serves the twofold purpose of conserving materials now vitally needed for the prosecution of the war and of building up a backlog of deferred civilian projects which will, in due time, be of considerable value in helping to cushion post-[DOT] war readjustments.
The foregoing remarks will, I trust, give some indication of the structure of the wartime industries control board, and of the scope of its activities. By reason of the board's existence, control measures proposed by any one controller have the benefit of consideration from all relevant aspects; orders when issued are not at cross purposes with those of other controllers; and, finally, the whole control programme is kept in line with its basic objective, which is the effective mobilization of economic resources.
Just to hurry on and finish my statement before six o'clock, I may add that Canada is, of course, producing munitions far in excess of the requirements of our own troops or the requirements for the defence of Canada. We are shipping these munitions to every area of warfare in the world. The largest shipments are, of course, to the United Kingdom, but very large shipments are being sent to the middle east, Russia, Australia, New Zealand, India, and South Africa; and during the campaign in Greece we sent large shipments to that country. We are very large shippers to China. The first aid received by China from North America, as Doctor Soong stated in a public address some time ago, came not from the United States but from Canada. It was a very substantial shipment of Bren guns, ammunition and some items of artillery. Since that time, every month has seen sizeable shipments made to China. We were also large shippers to Singapore, Malaya, Java and the Netherlands East Indies.
It seems to me that in the munitions programme Canada is taking part in the war on a world-wide scale. The main objective for Canada is to keep the war away from Canada. That, I think, is the only protection we have for our Canadian citizens. Therefore I think shipments of arms to China is a worth-while contribution to the defence of Canada. There are several hundred million Chinese people. For six or seven years they have been putting up a-splendid resistance to better equipped and 
better trained Japanese forces; and, properly armed, China is in a position to play a very important part in the future of this war. Again, I think our shipments to Russia have been worth while. Here also we have a population of some 160 million people fighting a most gallant battle against better equipped and perhaps better trained troops; and anything we can do to reinforce the effort of the Russian people is another way of keeping the war from Canada. The same thing applies to India. We have been a large shipper to that country since the beginning of the war, and we are continuing to send large shipments. Here again we have a large population immediately subject to attack, and here again we are in a position to defend Canada by sending arms to the other side of the world. I am happy to say we have made substantial contributions to our sister dominions, all of which are, I think, more immediately subject to attack than is Canada. I am always delighted when ve can make substantial shipments of arms, munitions and radio devices to those countries. Therefore, while we think of Canada's munitions effort as auxiliary to Canada's armed services, in a way those munitions are going to a wider front, in that they are playing a part on every battlefield of the war, than the nature of the war thus far has made it possible for our armed services to do.
I think this concludes what I have to say by way of statement, but when we reassemble I shall be very glad to explain any points in which hon. members may be interested.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at six o'clock the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) had just concluded a brief but rather comprehensive survey of the activities of his important department. We realize that probably at no time in the history of Canada has any department been charged with greater responsibilities than that of the Minister of Munitions and Supply at this particular time. The administration of his department involves responsibilities of tremendous dimensions and, as he has stated in his remarks, it indeed causes extensive repercussions on our whole economic system. To keep the wheels of our munitions and supply industries going is an unprecedented

War Appropriation-Supplies
challenge to our human and natural resources. However, it is with considerable alarm that one observes the tremendous financial obligations on our country that are involved.
As the minister has well said, it involves the coordination of control and the curtailment of civilian consumption. As he has stated, this is necessary if we are to wage an all-out war. The change from civilian consumption and production to war-time production is no small task. I am not going to discuss the details of the administration of his department because I realize that the minister has worked and laboured very hard. He has more than ordinary native ability; he has had long experience, and I know there are many contentious features to be met with in the administration of a department of that size. My only purpose in rising at this time is to offer such constructive help as I can to the government in order to create a better plan by which our people may play a fuller part in the gigantic task that now challenges every freedom-loving nation in the world.
If we are to justify our place in this democracy in which we live we must wage a total all-out war with all its bitter consequences. We must include in our many sacrifices the temporary surrender of personal privilege and accept more or less the regimentation of our total war necessities. Never in our country's history has our task been so clear; and, so long as our liberty stands at bay, Canada must march in war rather than stand in defence. It is agreed that the task of the Minister of Munitions and Supply to furnish all the machines, munitions and other equipment that our resources can supply as a striking force is fundamentally a responsibility of government.
As the minister has said alreadsq civilian consumption must be curtailed; indeed, civilian consumption must take what is left. The less we consume at home, the more we can fight abroad. We should not be satisfied with our war effort until we have a total output for war as high as it can be organized and a consumption of civilian goods at home as low as it can be endured. The extent to which we reach such objectives will reflect the greatness of the democratic way of life for which we fight. Amidst the blood, sweat, toil and tears that must be endured there at the present time is a glorious opportunity for this government to lead the country in reforms that will reduce inequalities of sacrifice in time of war as well as inequalities of happiness in the peace that we hope may soon follow. This cannot be achieved by merely meeting unexpected emergencies with hastily employed expediencies
It cannot be met either by a gunshot prescription of price fixing, rationing of goods, restricted sales, cramped business and high taxes.
The production of the necessary volume of munitions and supply creates subsequent problems for our whole economic system. We must have less chance and more design. Therefore, at this late date I hasten to urge the government to inaugurate a more basic war-time plan that may be more generally and universally applied to this gigantic problem. The mobilization of money as well as of men must be adopted. We have a two billion dollar vote before us now. We must find the money before we can produce the goods. Perhaps there are those who would prefer to call it conscription of wealth. However, many months ago I stated in this house that the government should have given consideration long ago to a policy of compulsory saving of a certain percentage of all the net wages and income above a reasonable living allowance. That is, above a reasonable living allowance for our people who are engaged in this great war problem.
May I, therefore, as I urge the government to take action again, be permitted to give a few reasons why I make this statement. First, I believe it would provide funds for the immediate prosecution of the war and the provision of the munitions and supply we are now discussing. Second, it would curtail as well the increasing purchasing power for nonessential civilian goods, referred to by the minister. Third, it would avoid inflation, and everybody shudders to think what inflation might do to our general economy. Fourth, it would more evenly distribute Canada's debt so that many war workers and soldiers would have, after the war, a source of income that they might not otherwise have. During the last year or two we have learned a good deal about the tendencies that are now developing.
In April last there appeared in the press a report by Mr. Spinney, chairman of the finance committee of Canada, with reference to our war loan issue. This statement announced that the final figures for the last victory loan which opened on February 16 showed that one out of 6-5 of Canada's population purchased bonds, whereas in the first victory loan in June, 1941, one out of every 12-02 bought bonds. Notwithstanding the fact that this loan was originally floated for $600,000,000 and then approached $900,000,000, this announcement is quite significant. It is indicative of the distress signal over controls already employed to check inflationary trends in our war economy.

Failure to recognize this could, to my mind, give rise to social and1 economic dislocations which, if allowed to continue, not only would impair the progress of our war eifort but might affect our whole democratic economy following the war. Increased employment coupled with Wages higher than those that prevailed prior to the war, and the huge governmental spending for armaments that we are now discussing, all create increased purchasing power at a time when the transition from peace-time to war-time economy is decreasing the supply of civilian goods which can be purchased. To meet this inflationary trend we have adopted measures of price fixing, wage and price controls, rationing and restriction of sales. All these measures, while they have in themselves contributed materially to curtail inflationary trends, do not measure up to the gigantic problem that is facing this country at the present time, which I fear is all too often lost sight of.
By means of increased taxation the government has endeavoured to divert as much as possible of the excess purchasing power created by huge government expenditures in almost every field of endeavour as a result of the war.
Notwithstanding the increased taxation and the prices and wage controls exercised by the government, there has been a very substantial increase in the real wages earned by Canadians since war began.
It would appear, Mr. Chairman, that the large group which has received large increases in purchasing power as a result of the war is not being effectively reached by our bond issues or our various war savings campaigns. A continuation of this situation is most dangerous to our economy because, unless some action is taken to reduce still further the increased purchasing power now in the hands of would-be purchasers, the .inflationary forces so much feared will become a reality. As time passes and our war effort progresses, the amount of consumer available goods will diminish, and at the same time government spending will be increasing tremendously.
The volume of goods for civilian consumption is at the present time below the 1933 level, whereas the national income this year is over twice the income level of 1933, due in no small degree to our production of munitions and supplies.
It is obvious that notwithstanding the measures of price freezing and wage control already
I Mr. Rowe.]
employed, further restrictions on the volume of purchasing power must be initiated if inflation is to be avoided.
The ever-widening gap between increased purchasing power in the hands of the public and the ever-diminishing supplies of consumer goods will have to be met by more effective measures. This can be approached either by increased taxes or compulsory savings, or by a combination of both; but some aggressive action must be taken to control the excess consumer purchasing power created by our war-time economy.
No one should expect to gain from the war in increased net returns from profits, dividends, rents, wages or prices. There can be little disagreement with this principle, which has been recognized in our excess profits tax policy. The wage earner or the business man, enjoying comparative safety in Canada, who may reluctantly pay new taxes and hesitate to lend his savings should pause and consider the many who are cheerfully offering their lives and hopes, without financial gain, to save this critical day. That everyone should pay something toward the cost of the war is, I believe, a principle acceptable to the Canadian people, because all should be willing to make their contribution toward bringing this conflict to a speedy and successful conclusion.
Excepting those whose standard of living is already at a low figure, I believe that every man, woman or child in Canada who has an income would willingly pay 5 to 10 per cent of it as a war contribution in the form of compulsory savings withheld at the source.
This money would then be made available to the government for the prosecution of the war and would be repayable to the individual in instalments during the period of rehabilitation that will follow the war.

While recent figures are not available, it is reasonable to assume that under our present accelerated war economy, coupled with the restrictions applied to control rents, dividends, et cetera, the percentage of the national income in the class of earned income is to-day a higher percentage than at any previous time in our history.
Any effort to reduce the purchasing power in the hands of the people must be directed toward where the national income is greatest, because the heart of any anti-inflation policy is the restriction of spending, particularly in non-essential consumer goods, by the great majority of our people, as well as by the 15 per cent of the few so-called "rich".
Recognition of this fact is evident by the campaign to induce the Canadian people to purchase war savings certificates. Doubtless there are a great many wage and salary earners who are not contributing in any measure to this effort, and it is unlikely that the voluntary appeal can achieve much greater results than the national objective of ten million dollars a month.
In war time compulsion is often a necessary step. While compulsion may be temporarily distasteful to a democratic people, it is necessary if a democratic people are to
succeed against a totalitarian group of nations where everything in the interest of the state is done by compulsion.
I would suggest to the government that consideration be given at once to the adoption of a policy of compulsory savings as an essential and integral part of our war supply policy.
This is important, not alone because of the revenue that would be made available for the immediate prosecution of the war, but as well in view of the anti-inflationary effect such a measure would have on our entire war economy. The principle of voluntary choice in the purchase of war savings certificates should be retained; indeed, the publicity campaign should be accelerated, so that every dollar that can be saved over and above what may be involved in a compulsory savings plan may be made a fighting dollar. The vital war obligation of the hour demands, however, that this economic necessity must not be left to chance or voluntary choice alone.
Our present voluntary plan should accordingly be supplemented by a general loan levy, such as I have proposed, not only to increase the government fighting loans for to-day, but to equalize the war savings of our people for to-morrow. We have endeavoured to control inflationary trends by measures of price and wage controls, but these constitute only half-measures to cure inflation, and do nothing to prevent the disease itself. Unless compulsion is exercised to curtail this increasing tide of purchasing power, it is doubtful that the tremendous problems confronting us can be controlled. I would suggest to the government that legislation be introduced at this session of parliament to make operative by July 1 next a policy of compulsory savings, deductible at the source of income and repayable in instalments after the war.

While such a measure would entail considerable administrative detail work, the larger part of this work could be done by the employer in a manner similar to the national defence tax deductions now made at the source. The advantages of such a policy would be many.
First, this would constitute a definite antiinflation step because the increased purchasing power would be withheld at the source. Second, the amount withheld would be in the form of non-transferable savings, repayable after the war. Third, repayments could be made in instalments during the period of rehabilitation when the war wage-earner might be unemployed and in need of state assistance. Furthermore, such a policy would give the wage-earner a certain security for the future, rather than permitting a limited few to hold the bonds of Canada's increased debt.
To make savings a compulsory deduction from eveiy source of earned income in specific percentages would have the effect of making everybody contribute something for the prosecution of the war. The money raised would, through compulsory savings, be available to the government and would take the place of money loaned from chartered banks. This is important because it would place as much as possible of the federal debt in the hands of the people outside the chartered banks. A payroll deduction plan would assure a steady flow of funds for the prosecution of the war; it would cut down consumer spending, and, in the final analysis, it is the soundest kind of savings plan for the individual. The withholding of income at the source would assist in shifting our material and human resources to military uses without creating an excessive demand for non-essential civilian goods. It would mean the purchase of savings certificates from income rather than from accumulated savings in the banks as has been the practice in the past. The purchase of savings certificates from income rather than from accumulated savings would leave more money for the banks to purchase government bonds if the need should arise. It would provide the best means of building up national security for the element of our people most likely to need assistance during the post-war period of adjustment which must be anticipated.
I realize the problems of the government. I have endeavoured to give constructive assistance to the minister and to the government in the heavy task that is theirs at this time. However, as I conclude may I be permitted to warn the government of certain dangers in the trends that are being established by the expediencies with which emergencies are being met, and have to be met, from day to day.
[Mr. Rowe.l
Since before the fall of the Roman empire the lesson has been plain that economic liberty and civil liberty stand or fall together. We must, therefore, preserve as much freedom of choice for the individual consumer as it is possible to preserve in our way of life.
Universal price fixing and rationing, and all these regulations of a totalitarian and bureaucratic nature which we are now developing as expediencies to meet these emergencies, are to no small extent a product of totalitarianism itself; but that is not so in so far as Canada is concerned, and we do not want them to be the introduction to totalitarianism. I do not believe that we as a people who are fighting for democratic freedom should let a totalitarian system take root so deeply in this country that it will eventually destroy democratic freedom itself.
Even if such uncertain schemes were successful enough to control consumption completely, as the Minister of Munitions and Supply has indicated is his desire, so that a substantial fraction of our earned incomes could not be spent, the result would not be different-only more extravagant than if the incomes had been deferred from the outset, as I have suggested.
Accordingly, with a more limited purchasing power that would be brought about by such a policy, more free choice could be left with the individual. It would not be necessary for the government to ask the housewife to be a detective watching over her neighbour's consumption and purchases of her daily bread. In other words, it would tend to enable us to maintain through this crisis those basic principles that have enabled freedom of enterprise and individual initiative to give life and vigour to our democratic progress.
I urge the government in all fairness to give careful consideration to what, to my mind, is a basic essential in this war, a war-time plan which we have not yet had. It is all very well to organize an industry, all very well to get high-class dollar-a-year men here to carry on an industry, but we must find ways and means to maintain that industry. As the minister well said this afternoon, part of his duty is to mobilize all the great natural resources of this country, but if we are to mobilize them soundly I believe we had better start at the root of the trouble and meet these realities. Then we shall have a more effective way of financing the war and a sounder way of meeting after-the-war problems.

I do not intend to follow the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) in the argument he has advanced this evening, but I believe the ideas which he has placed before the committee merit the most serious consideration of the government.

War Appropriation-Supplies
My purpose in saying a few words at this time is generally to open the subject of munitions and supply with a view to obtaining some information from the minister regarding his department.
At the outset I commend him for the advances which have taken place during the past year. Munitions from Canada have found their way to the battlefields of China and Russia, and, as he says, to every allied front in the world. This afternoon he uttered one thought which I wish were understood all over this dominion, namely, that our duty as a country to-day is not to await the coming of the enemy to our gates but to see to it, as a nation and a parliament, that the enemy is kept from our gates. He has related some of the actions taken by the government and some of the drastic changes which have occurred.
The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe has mentioned the necessity of a curtailment of civilian purchases. I realize that there has been an expansion in munitions production since the war, that to-day 600,000 men and women are engaged- in war production, and that about one million people are employed now who were not employed at the outbreak of the war. But one significant matter which must not be lost sight of is that we have 337,000 men and women in industry, supplying civilian requirements and wants, in addition to those who were so employed at the outbreak of war.
He told of the curtailments which were necessary to preserve rubber and gasoline. I could understand that there might be some who would raise objection thereto, but I have not yet heard of them. The people of Canada are ready for curtailments; they are ready to accept drastic reductions in their way of living; they are ready to make sacrifices; but they demand a lead on the part of the government. I believe that the attitude of the people to-day is that it is time for Canada to get tough. It is time to do things we have not done before, to the end that our efforts, our maximum efforts,- shall be canalized or centralized into the war effort. In connection with aeroplane production-and that is what I will deal with in the main this evening-we should consider the question of immediate expansion. I will not go into a survey of what the minister has said, or an analysis of his speech. Before doing so, I shall wait until to-morrow when I shall have had an opportunity of reading in detail what he said. Let me point out, however, that if he is optimistic for 1942 and 1943, he was just as optimistic in 1940 and 1941, and yet he has to come to-day before
this committee and say that some of the promises he then made were not justified by subsequent developments.

December 20, 1941.
Mr. E. G. Hirst of Toronto has just undertaken the responsibility of organizing and conducting a morale-building campaign m the aircraft and allied industries through the year 1942, and I bespeak your whole-hearted cooperation for him in making this campaign an outstanding success.	.
Mr. Hirst will act as chairman of a dominionwide committee and will probably associate local committees in each community where work of this character is to be carried out.
It is estimated that the work will involve Mr. Hirst being absent from his own business at least three-quarters of his time, and his volume is therefore bound to suffer.
I have pointed out that his position is vice-president of Might Directories of Toronto.
If you can, therefore, place with Mr. Hirst your printing account for the year, it should go a long way toward maintaining sufficient volume in his own business, so that he will not have to worry, and I would appreciate your sympathetic and generous consideration of his interest in this connection, it being understood, of course, that any business _ sp placed with him will be on a strictly competitive basis.
I ask you, what business has a department of government to call upon private manufacturers to give their printing to a private individual, whether on a competitive basis or otherwise?
But that is not all.
In order to cover his out-of-pocket expenses for travelling, organizing and such office assistance as is required I have put your firm down for the amount noted at the foot of this letter.
Some got put down for $500, many others for $250. There are eight put down for $500 and the rest to make up $9,000 at $250 each.
Will you please send your cheque for this amount to Mr. P. C. Garratt, Managing Director, de Havilland Aircraft of Canada, Ltd., Postal Station L, Toronto. Mr. Garratt has kindly consented to act as honorary treasurer of the dominion committee. All Mr. Hirst's bills will be paid on behalf of the industry only through Mr. Garratt.
Authorizing a private individual to go out in order to build up morale for which services he is to be paid by donations from the different aircraft manufacturers, and in addition to which he is to get their printing "upon a competitive basis," is bad enough. But the next paragraph is the one to which I raise the most strenuous objection, and which in my opinion shows whether or not the answer given in this house on May 6 was in fact correct:
This sum is, by arrangement with treasury, chargeable to overhead in connection with your aircraft contracts.
The companies were to pay out $500 or $250, as the case may be, and they were to give their printing to him "on a competitive basis"; but they are not to be out anything on the contributions made; the people of Canada are going to pay it. And these men were to conceal payments under "overhead." Why the necessity to cover it up? Why not appoint Mr. Hirst in charge of this very commendable work as director of morale and put him on a salary? But no; it is not done in that way. The aeroplane companies are
War Appropriation-Supplies

told to pad up or add up the amount in their overhead and to charge it to the treasury of Canada.
The letter goes on:
Most of you will realize that the work which Mr. Hirst is now taking over has, in the past, necessitated a considerable portion of my time which should be devoted to other matters. I am sure that with someone now able to give practically full time to this work, this important phase of personnel relations will receive an impetus that will be felt throughout the entire industry, and I know that I can count on you to give Mr. Hirst every possible help and assistance.
Let each of us individually and all of us collectively determine that 1942 is going to produce results in the aircraft field that will literally amaze this country.
Cordially yours,
_	Ralph R. Bell,
Director-General of Aircraft Production.
There is a letter from "Phil"; it does not say who he is, but evidently the managing director of the de Havilland Aircraft of Canada Limited. It is dated January 3, 1942, addressed to Mr. Bell. He says:
In connection with the Morale-Building Campaign and the activities of Mr. E. G. Hirst!
I would like a little bit clearer outline of the activities, if that is at all possible, just in order that as far as I am concerned I will not be deviating from your policy.
One question I have been asked so far is who the officers might be, if I am the honorary treasurer.
Up to the present time about $4,000 have tumbled into the coffers and Mr. Hirst has engaged an office at $40 a month, is procuring furniture, and I have advanced him $150 on account of expenses. I presume this is all in order and that I am just to comply with whatever requests Mr. Hirst makes.
Then there is a letter to Mr. Garratt directing him:
You will pay out to Mr. E. G. Hirst money on his requisitions.
Why was this house and this committee not given the information when it asked for it on May 6? Why was it necessary to conceal from the people the fact that Mr. Hirst's $9,000 expense account was coming out of the treasury of Canada? I should like the minister to explain this. I can understand, as the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe said, that in the interests of the war effort it may be necessary to depart from some of the ordinary democratic principles. It is necessary to set up controllers; but I do insist that whoever is set up as a controller shall remain responsible to parliament. I do insist that no controller whose salary is concealed in the overhead expenses of those producing aircraft or other products shall draw money from the coffers of the people of Canada. I am going to ask the minister. IMr. Diefenbaker.J
when he explains the circumstances in connection with this matter, whether it is or is not a fact that there are others in the position of Mr. Hirst. The reason why I ask that question is this. If the opposition had accepted the answers that were given on May 6, no one in this house or in this country ever would have known that Mr. Hirst was drawing $9,000 as expenses. It all would have been concealed. The only thing known about him wovdd have been that he was a man who was giving ^ his services to the high purpose of increasing and extending aircraft production in Canada. I think parliament has a right to be assured that steps such as this, which constitute an advance toward a hidden bureaucracy, no longer will be tolerated; and I ask the minister to give the assurance that answers such as were given on May 6, 1942, no longer will be permitted, for in my opinion answers such as those fail to reveal the true circumstances and are an affront to parliament itself. If we cannot ask for information, without the necessity of having everything at hand to check up and see whether it is correct, as an opposition we only play act; we can only go on fishing expeditions, depending on the government to give us answers that are correct. Carry on that sort of thing very long, Mr. Chairman, and we will need a morale minister in this government to convince the people of Canada that all answers being given are in accordance with the facts.
I ask why it was necessary to go beyond the ranks of the civil service, to hunt up a man whose qualifications were that the published a directory, in order to build up morale in Canada? We have a Department of National War Services under which we have all the various branches dealing with public information, radio and all those other organizations that furnish information, whose purpose is to instil and maintain morale among our people. Why was it necessary to go outside a department of government to secure the services of a man whose qualifications, according to the record, do not appear to be such as would contribute much to. morale in the aircraft industry? Why was it necessary for a department of government to answer that this man was not receiving any salary, that he was receiving no emolument or consideration whatsoever? I ask the minister to give this house and the country a frank explanation in regard to this most unusual case.

Well, Mr. Chairman, my
lion, friend has given the committee quite a display of histrionics over a rather simple matter. I was told some time ago about this matter. I may say I discovered the letter

I rise to a point

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
I said it was handed to a
member of the hon. gentleman's party, and the leader of that party told me two hours ago that he had it, confirming information which I received' some time ago. So on a point of order I would ask that my hon. friend keep his seat until I finish this explanation.

I think

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: I think so. To continue, Mr. Chairman, I heard about this letter some time ago. Naturally my reaction was somewhat similar to that of the hon. member for Lake Centre. It is one of those things that occur, and after it is discovered you only do what you can about it. I made very sure that no insurance was placed as suggested in the letter, and I also made sure that the payments would not become an element of overhead cost on the part of any of the subscribers.

When was that,
may I ask?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
That was some two months
ago, as I remember it, or perhaps a month ago.
Before May 6?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply

to parliament is dated May 6.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply

speechtext: Just paid by it.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Just a moment; I would appreciate it if I could make my statement.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
The situation is that the letter was written some time ago. I heard of it two or three months after the letter was written. As I say, I took such steps as I could to set the matter straight. The question that was asked was handled by the department in the ordinary way. An officer of our department is assigned to the duty of furnishing information in reply to these questions. He obtains his information from the records of the department. The name of the gentleman in question, Mr. Hirst, does not appear in the records of the department; but I suppose my officer dug around and found that this man was employed by the industry, so he gave the answer accordingly. I hand in these answers, naturally assuming them to be correct;
I do not personally go through the records of the department. The answer is correct, according to the information in the records of the department. The explanation I received from the director of aircraft production, when the letter was produced, was that the industry had decided that work of the kind for which Mr. Hirst was employed was necessary.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Why was
it necessary?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
I do not know that it is necessary7. I may say that if I had been asked to make this as an official appointment, I would not have made it. I do not believe in this kind of propaganda in an industry. However, it was represented to me that the industry decided this was a desirable thing to do. I was told that certain members of the industry-I do not say that all were represented- agreed to contribute to the expenses of this man. Had the payment been sponsored by anyone but the director-general of aircraft production I would have found very little to criticize about it, but obviously the director-general of aircraft production should not have had any part in the payment of a man to be employed at the expense of the industry.
I am quite willing to say that the letter was a wholly improper letter. As I say, I considered it as such and I did what I could to correct the situation. I am bound to say that my department is not made up of experienced civil servants; it is made up of men from industry, men who have a different point of view from that of men with experience in the public service. I could have
War Appropriation-Supplies

done two things. I could have dismissed my director-general of aircraft production because I thought he had done an improper act or, on the other hand-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Nobody has suggested that.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: What else could I do except what I did? I had to weigh the fact that he came in full of enthusiasm, took an industry that was moribund at the time and built it up into a most excellent industry to-day. It has expanded by forty times. But his methods are not always the methods that I would have used. I am more methodical generally than my director-general of aircraft production; nevertheless I do not know that I could have made as good a job of that industry had I taken it over at the time he did. We have the facts. There is no use in trying to explain the inexplicable or to excuse the inexcusable. That letter was a most improper letter; nevertheless it was written, and written without my knowledge. As I say, I learned about it some two months later, and I did what I could to straighten out the situation. Money had been collected, and the man was at work and apparently doing a very good job. He was working with the industry and at the expense of the industry. I see nothing to get hysterical about. These things happen, I suppose. This is a most unpleasant incident, and if my hon. friend has any suggestions as to what I should do about it at this stage, I shall be very glad to take them into consideration.

Now that the minister has made his explanation, the answer that was given on May 6 does become inexplicable. The question asked then was, "If no remuneration is paid to him by the government, by what means is he being compensated for his services?" The answer was, "He is receiving no compensation for his services".
From the government.
Yes, from the government, when all the charges that were made were ultimately paid by the people of Canada by an addition to overhead in the contracts?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: They are deductible from overhead.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: No; they are not. They were at the start, but they are not now.

I just want to ask the minister one question. If he stopped this thing, where are the letters putting an 
end to it? The last letter is dated January 15, at which time $4,000 had tumbled into the coffers. What has happened to that $4,000? Has it been returned to the aircraft companies? In whose possession is it to-day? Possibly the minister will be able to explain what does not appear in the record.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
