speechtext: I explained that I stopped any possibility of any advertising being diverted, and I also stopped any deductions being made, or any charges being made against overhead on this account. As I said, the money had been paid in part, and it had been expended on this campaign which is still going on and which is still going to expand. As far as the answer from the department is concerned, I have told how it happened. I said that my hon. friend asked a trick question and his trick worked. He got the answer he expected.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I do not think the question was a trick question.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: He had the letter in his hand.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: And I do not think the answer was a very candid answer. The whole thing is a most regrettable incident.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Quite.
The minister said that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Will the hon. member hold himself in patience? The minister asked for certain suggestions, and I rose to give them to him. It is a most regrettable incident. It was a matter of indiscretion on the part of a gentleman whose friendship I have held for many years and who has done, in my view, a most wonderful work in connection with aircraft production in Canada. Let that be said. However, his methods in respect of expenditures are not just according to Hoyle. Perhaps without being concerned, or, shall I say, without realizing the implications of the statement that subscriptions made to the fund could be recouped by deductions from overhead, he endeavoured to raise this money. While the government was not paying anything directly, it was paying the full $9,000 indirectly.
This letter came to us from one of the manufacturers who paid because he felt he dare not refuse, and on its receipt the first question I asked myself was: why was it necessary to build up morale in the aircraft industry in Canada? The minister has not yet elucidated that point. I do not know what the necessity was. Was there strife in the industry? Was not there full cooperation on the part of the

War Appropriation-Supplies
men in the industry? My impression is that the men in this industry are among the best paid in Canada. I have sent many boys from my community in New Brunswick to Montreal to engage in this industry. Universally they have been successful, and many of them are making very high wages to-day. What was the necessity for building up morale? The minister says that there was not any necessity, and he ought to know. My first suggestion to the minister is that Mr. Hirst should go back and attend to his knitting, which is the building up of a directory in the city of Toronto.
I approve the minister's action entirely in seeing to it that not one dollar of this money shall be paid out of the national treasury by an indirect method. I give my unqualified approval to that. The next suggestion I make is that this money or that part of it which has not been spent be returned to the industry. Then I think the chapter can be closed.
In view of the answers that were given to questions asked earlier this month, I really was surprised to see that we got the correspondence as we did. But the correspondence was brought down, and it was a proper return to make to the motion. One thought that naturally arises in one's mind is this: In connection with government industry or industry engaged on large government contracts, is this the first or isolated case in which this practice has been pursued? I do not know. If it is not, I should like the minister to give an undertaking that this sort of thing will stop and stop immediately. If it is necessary to do a job in industry in order to build up morale, if it is necessary to do any kind of job in industry, there is ample opportunity to appoint men to do that and to pay them an honest wage. I would not object at all if it were established that a morale building campaign were necessary in the aircraft industry. Then an appointment should be made of a proper man under the proper circumstances, and he should be paid a salary and expenses out of the public treasury. I would assume that those who appointed him, those who understood the necessity for the appointment, those who understood the necessity for the operation, would believe that it was in the public interest to do so. That is the open, candid way to do this sort of thing. I must say that I am as regretful as the minister that anything like this occurred.
I should like to have the minister's assurance that, as far as he can prevent it, nothing of this kind will ever occur again, and that if it has occurred in connection with other persons who have contractual rights with the government, the practice will be stopped immediately. Eveiy hon. member within sound of my voice
knows this, that men engaged in operations for the government, when a request of this kind or something similar in scope comes to them, are afraid to say no for fear it will injure their business. There are manufacturers who are afraid to come to my office to see me for fear that even a social visit may be misconstrued. That ought not to be.
Tell them it is not so.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I try to tell them so, but they say: "I wish you well but I cannot come because I am engaged on a government contract." I do not say that there is any system of espionage or any system set up whereby these men would become marked men. But human nature is human nature.
You are too guarded.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Maybe I am, and other people may not be so guarded. But it is true that people are afraid to give me information on this very matter. I do not regard this as a major instance, but I do regard it as a very regrettable instance, and I am glad to have the minister's assurance that it will never occur again. But I ask him to go further than he has suggested and to see that this money is returned. It ought all to be returned, and Mr. Hirst, if he is not required, should be sent back to his own business. Furthermore, no scheme of this kind should be permitted to be carried on by any official of the government. I am sure that no civil servant would do it, and no experienced agent of the government and in its employ should do it, because I think we are all agreed that it is not the right method to pursue. H the minister will take the proper steps to correct the position, he will hear no more about it from me.

Mr. Chairman, we listened with a great deal of interest to the statement made by the Minister of Munitions and Supply this afternoon, and I believe that most members were pleased to hear of the great strides which have been made in producing in this country munitions of war. I want at the outset to compliment the minister upon what has been accomplished under him in his department.
May I, however, say to him and the committee, that if there is some uneasiness in the minds of some members of parliament and of many outside this house throughout Canada, it is because in this year of life-and-death struggle a considerable feeling exists that we are not doing all we should and can do. There are many lines of munitions production in which we have perhaps reached,
War Appropriation,-Supplies

shall I say, our peak, blit there are other lines in which we have not. Some time ago when I asked a question of the minister, on the orders of the day, regarding the building of wooden ships he was extremely curt with me -I say that in all kindliness-and told me that the question of building wooden ships was a closed book. On May 9, the evening Citizen of Ottawa contained an article which, I believe, sets out the viewpoint of many of us regarding the building of ships of all kinds. It is by A. C. Cummings and comes from London. Here is the viewpoint of the people of Great Britain regarding Canada's shipbuilding programme:
London

Expansion of Canada's shipbuilding programme to 172 vessels with a three-shift working day on the Pacific coast is welcomed in Great Britain, for no need is greater among the united nations this spring than that of ships-more and yet more ships.
Shipping is the key to the whole allied strategy just now. Given plenty of ships Japan could be checked in the Pacific within a few months. Ships carry fighter aircraft and if there were enough of these in the far eastern war zone the enemy could not hope to invade either India or Australia.
Ships carry troops and tanks, too-and these are wanted all over the globe.
It takes five tons of shipping to convey a British soldier and his mechanized equipment overseas. Some units have to travel thirteen thousand miles-six months out and back for a convoy.
Unfortunately, Britain began the war short of ships, for in 1935 seven million tons-more than the Japanese have had for their huge conquests in the Pacific-were considered "redundant", that is, could not earn freights and so were sold, broken up or otherwise disposed of. At the same time, British shipyards were "rationalized", which meant, in plain language, that they were dismantled and shut down. To-day, because of this and because the United Kingdom has to concentrate on new warships, Britain's output of cargo-carriers is only about one million tons.
True, the United States shipbuilding programme is immense and a year hence will be of enormous aid to the allies.
But the urgent need of the moment is ships now-this spring-and although construction in the British empire and the United States combined is already roughly equivalent to sinkings in the Battle of the Atlantic and in the Pacific, what is wanted is to double the present output.
"At this time we could do with literally millions more tons of ships", a high authority told me.	"Every ton that comes from a
Canadian shipyard this year is worth more than five tons a year hence."
This afternoon the minister placed on record a statement regarding the building of steel ships in Canada and, of course, we are doing a splendid job in the building of these vessels. I may be wrong, but I am of the belief that because of the great shipbuilding programme of the United States and, shall I say, with the limited output of steel, it will not be possible
[Mr. Beid.l
to expand our steel shipbuilding programme much further than what is now being done. I have here a statement made by Admiral Land of the United States, and I just wish that some of our people and officials in this country were imbued with the same spirit. Referring to the United States shipbuilding programme, which contemplates building 2,900 ships in 300 days, Admiral Land was reminded that these ships might not last long. He swore when he was reminded that the ships now being built by the United States might not last five years, and he said, "We will take the goods across to Great Britain if we have to row them over there. I don't care a damn how long the ships last. Our duty is to build the ships so that Great Britain may be supplied with all the goods she requires."
We have on both our coasts, but particularly in British Columbia, many men available for wooden shipbuilding. When I was out on the Pacific coast at Easter I paid a visit to many manufacturing plants, and I found queues o,f men waiting to put down their names for work. True, most of the artisans have been picked up and are at work in machine-shops and in our steel shipyards; but when I think that during the last war in British Columbia we had twenty-seven shipyards operating, four of them building steel ships as well as wooden ships on the Fraser river, and to-day we have only a total of seventeen operating, I just wonder whether we are doing all we can to build ships with which to carry our products to the beleaguered people of Great Britain. While I am not going to make a definite charge against the officials of the minister's department, I am going to lay a serious complaint against what has happened, and I am going to give one instance of what has kept orders from British Columbia, while orders for wooden ships are being placed in the United States.
Just before I left home at Easter, those connected with the shipbuilding industry of British Columbia, and particularly with the building of wooden ships, asked me if I would meet them in conference, which I did in Vancouver on the day I left. They made the definite statement that some official in Ottawa of the Department of Munitions and Supply had been asked by the British authorities if British Columbia, Canada, could build wooden mine-sweepers, and the official from Great Britain was told by Canadian officials that it could not be done. Later, this British official whilst in New York discussed the matter with United States officials, and was told that wooden mine-sweepers could be built on the United States Pacific coast. What is happening now is this: fifty miles from the border, south

War Appropriation-Supplies
of Vancouver, at the city of Bellingham, wooden mine-sweepers are being built to the order of the British government, and British Columbia is supplying most of the lumber.
Is that true?

That charge was made by six shipbuilders. I asked if I could make that charge, and they said, "Yes, you can make that charge-that a British official came to Ottawa with a view of placing orders for wooden mine-sweepers, and was told that British Columbia could not build wooden minesweepers, and to-day there are seventy wooden mine-sweepers being built in the United States, mainly on the Pacific coast, and we are supplying most of the lumber for the building of those ships." I say in all seriousness that if that statement is true-and these men gave it to me on good authority, because they had spent a long time in Ottawa endeavouring to procure orders for British Columbia-it is most serious. I am drawing this to the attention of the minister; but particularly do I want him to view this war in a different aspect and not close his mind against the building of wooden ships. We have men who can build ships in plenty. Hundreds of men are idle in British Columbia who could go into these wooden shipyards and help to construct these vessels. We have lumber in abundance. With a statement such as I have given, and in the light of the crying need for ships of every kind, we need not tell the people of British Columbia or the people of the country in general that we are doing everything we can to help Great Britain and help our allies, in this war.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
There seems to be some confusion when we talk about wooden ships. We are building wooden ships; we have been building them since the first day of the war. What we were discussing a year ago was wooden cargo ships, which is a particular class of ship. We have not built wooden cargo ships. The difference between a wooden cargo ship and a'steel cargo ship is largely in the material which makes the hull. There is very little difference in the material which goes into the boilers, the engines, the steering gear and various other fittings. The question is, is it good business to build steel hulls or wooden hulls? That is the question in regard to the cargo boats. All our experts tell me that there is more value in the steel hull. I have said that if we could augment the work in any way and if we could find a user for wooden cargo ships, we would be pleased to make them. I have made that offer quite freely. I asked the private trade, if they wanted to
enter into a lease-operating arrangement for wooden ships, to let us know, and I received no offers; I have had no interest from any 3hip user in wooden ships. Obviously, my department builds for someone, and we can hardly build wooden ships unless we can find someone who wants those ships.
Wooden mine-sweepers, wooden Fairmile boats and wooden tugs are quite a different matter. We build them. We have been building them. No officer of mine could possibly have told my hon. friend that these could not be built on the Pacific coast because we have been building them for a long time. My officers are quite familiar with what can be done, and so are the British. British shipbuilding experts go every month to British Columbia. An admiralty mission has been resident in Canada for a year and a half; they know Canada as well as I do. I suggest to my hon. friend that he should not make a statement like the one he has made unless he can give me the name of the officer and afford me a chance to trace it down. If he will do that, that is all right. But if it is simply a sweeping statement that some officer said so-and-so, I would say that that could not possibly be so, because my officers are familiar with both coasts and have arranged for a great deal of shipbuilding to be done on both coasts.

I have been in this house since 1930, and I have never made a statement which I could not back up. The minister asks for the name. Would the committee grant me this courtesy, that I supply the name in confidence to the minister rather than put it on Hansard?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: No; put it on Hansard.
I know how difficult it is for the official, how unfair it is just to blame the official and place the name on Hansard. But I have it with me.
Give it to the minister.

It is strange that we are only now beginning to think of building minesweepers in British Columbia, seeing that orders for seventy for the British admiralty have been placed in the United States for some considerable time. Can the minister tell us if the statement appearing in the press is correct that they are going to build thirty-five mine-sweepers in British Columbia? We can get no confirmation, and it is a very important matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
I cannot say at the moment, but I should be glad to make inquiries.

War Appropriation-Supplies

I listened this afternoon with some degree of pride as the minister told us of the efforts which have been put forward by his department on behalf of Canada and of the other allied countries of the world. But I have one matter in mind which I think should not be lost sight of. We are to a large degree losing responsible government in this dominion. In my opinion, responsible government by the elected representatives of the people has been largely superseded and control handed over to the dollar-a-year men who are big business men in this country. The other day I read a return from which it appears that there are 272 dollar-a-year men now handling the affairs of Canada. Many of them have very considerable interests of their own, and the tendency of such appointments is to establish in this country a bureaucracy, which has many dangerous aspects.
I rose, however, to ask a question or two pertaining to gasoline. The minister said that in the matter of gasoline the prairie provinces were more or less self-sufficient. In that respect, in the part of the country in which I live, one of the most prominent oil companies in Canada is running a very large fleet of trucks from Moose Jaw through southern Saskatchewan and southern Manitoba, delivering its products to distributing stations in that manner and paralleling the railroads. At a time like this, to say the least, this is a very bad example to other people who are asked to save gasoline and tires. I believe there are tank cars available on the railways, but this great fleet of trucks comes down the highways every day delivering their product on that basis. I trust the minister will be able to explain that.
Then there is the matter of the sale of gasoline from seven in the morning to seven in the evening. I do not know whether he realizes what that means to the agriculturists of the prairie provinces at this time of year and from now till the snow flies next fall, but in any centre in the prairie provinces, most of these people usually do their trading on Saturday evenings. That is the time when they go to town to do their shopping and buy their gasoline. I have not any idea what number of man-power hours would be saved to agriculture in the western provinces if they were allowed to purchase their gasoline until nine or ten o'clock on Saturday evening, but certainly it would be a good deal. I have received many resolutions from cooperatives asking that the hours of sale be extended for their benefit, at least on Saturday evenings. As I say, throughout

the entire prairie provinces agriculturists have to quit their work early in the day in order to reach their trading centres to procure gasoline before seven o'clock. It would be a great saving and immensely help our war effort if on Saturday evenings the hours of sale could be extended until nine or ten o'clock. I am sure that by this time the minister must have some information on the matter, if he would care to give it now.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: I shall be glad to call my hon. friend's remarks to the attention of the oil controller.

I want to make a few remarks with regard to wooden minesweepers. Either there is some misunderstanding or some difficulty must have been found in British Columbia which has not been experienced on the Atlantic coast. We have on the Atlantic coast building for the British admiralty, I believe, some thirty mine-sweepers. A number are being constructed in two yards in my constituency.
I am told that British Columbia is supplying lumber for these.
I do know about supplying the lumber. The lumber that goes into these mine-sweepers is coming in large measure from the districts in which the minesweepers are being built.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
The hon. member for New
Westminster (Mr. Reid) referred to the great many men unemployed in British Columbia. I should like to get to the bottom of that. I receive alarming reports of the shortage of operators in the aeroplane spruce industry. I suppose there is no more vital industry in connection with aeroplane production in this country than the aeroplane spruce industry. I am told1 that only 40 per cent of the required cutters in that industry can be engaged in British Columbia. The production of copper in British Columbia dropped' very sharply in the last two months and is still dropping, again through the shortage of men in the mines of the province. I receive complaints from various industries in British Columbia that the cut will be short this year because of a shortage of workers. Let us not talk glibly about the great unemployment in British Columbia.

The minister need not try to
be discourteous to me by saying that I am talking glibly. There has been a shift of labour in British Columbia. I know that, when I left, there were in one yard seventy-five men who were idle. I visited the Boeing aeroplane plant, and I could hardly get near

War Appropriation-Supplies
the desk, because such a great number of men and women were endeavouring to register.
I visited three plants, and some told me that they had as many as 250 men on the list. There are vacancies in the woods. Many of these men have been coming to the shipyards, but that does not dispose of the statement I made, and it was not a glib statement.

I wish to return to the
question raised by the member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker). There was one point in Mr. Bell's letter that was quite disturbing to me. I quite appreciate what the minister said about the condition in his department. I have been complaining about it for the last two years. These business men who are manning his department have been running their own business as they jolly well pleased for years and there was no one to say them nay. They expect now to do the same thing with the government's business. Their attitude has been a constant bone of contention since the war began, and I have not been able to get any satisfaction when I have complained of it. In Mr. Bell's letter I find this sentence:
This sum is, by arrangement with treasury, chargeable to overhead in connection with your aircraft contracts.
I was on the war expenditures committee last year. I was on committee No. 1 that went into the matter of treasury control, and we were given to understand that everything was so iron-clad that one could not get a nickel past the treasury. The members of the treasury department are there for the purpose of protecting the interests of the people of Canada as represented by the crown, and, unless they consulted with the minister-and even if they had consulted with him-were not looking after their business in the proper way, when they would allow an arrangement of this kind to be made. It seems to me that this is a most serious charge against the officials of the treasury. They certainly failed in their duty when they allowed an item of this kind to be covered up in overhead. They are being paid to see that such a thing does not happen, and no controller or anyone else should be able to tell any industry that he has made an arrangement with the treasury department that you can hide this or that amount in your costs. We should have fuller explanation of this than we have had.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
I am not the minister in
charge of treasury.

I have tried to look through Hansard, but I have not had time. I should like to refer to the remarks made
by the minister in connection with spruce. It is to our credit, and it is to the advantage of Canada, that we happen to have a monopoly in Sitka spruce, which is most essential for aeroplane wings, particularly bombers. The third largest logging concern in British Columbia is threatened with a shut-down to-day, and that is something of serious consequence to that province, though it is not half as serious to that province as it is to the dominion and to the war effort as a whole. The reason, as I gather from information that came to hand no later than yesterday, is the fact that the logging concerns, which, I suppose, are expected to produce at a normal profit, just as any other business does, are not able to compete with the shipyards in the right of way for labour. It has been questioned that there is any shortage of labour in that province in view of the fact that there are men who are unemployed. Does the minister expect that a logger will go up to Queen Charlotte islands-and there is no harder work in Canada than logging- when he can get the wages that are being paid in the shipyards on the cost-plus basis? The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), I suppose, knows better than I do about these matters, but I do not believe, from my own personal knowledge, the stories that are going around that the shipyard employers are leaning against one another. Work in a shipyard is a far easier form of employment than logging on Queen Charlotte islands.
The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) pointed out that we have not had orders for building minesweepers. In 1940 it was pointed out by five different members from British Columbia that we had all the materials; that we had unemployed, skilled and otherwise, in that province, and that we were capable of building these ships. If my memory serves me aright, the idea was pooh-poohed that we could build suitable wooden ships in that province. When it is said that because we have unemployment it should not be necessary to shut down logging, to me that does not make sense. Everyone cannot be a logger. I am sure the minister is not aware of the fact that in one riding in British Columbia to-day there are over fifty lathes idle, with all the mechanics to man them. Plant after plant has not been turning a wheel in that province. We have heard about total war effort and a shortage of power, shortage of gas and so on in other parts of Canada. I repeat, in one riding, there are over fifty lathes standing idle, with mechanics to man them and ample power going to waste. I do not think the minister is justified in his statement. The hon. member for New Westminster needs no assistance from me to defend him,
War Appropriation-Supplies

but the minister is not justified in his statement, and I say that speaking for my own riding and I have authority to speak for that riding at any rate until such time as the people there decide to send someone else here. I say unequivocally that in my opinion and in the opinion of my riding there is no total war effort in Canada when hundreds of skilled mechanics are unemployed and their lathes standing idle in British Columbia. That being so, we are not at total war, and nobody can convince me that we are.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: I am sorry to disagree with my hon. friend, but I cannot feel terribly upset about a condition of unemployment when our essential industries in British Columbia cannot operate to capacity, and needed capacity to make the war go, because they cannot get men.

If the minister would like, I can give him dates and names. I do not like to do this for the simple reason mentioned in other cases; human nature being what it is, it is quite possible that these firms might be discriminated against. But I -have the dates when these firms appeared before what is known as the "bits and pieces" department, although as far as British Columbia is concerned that is not the name I would use for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: All right.

I am expressing the opinion of my riding, and I am entitled to do so. That riding is as much concerned in this war effort as any other riding in Canada. It is just as patriotic, as is proved by the voluntary enlistments to date. When I am told that this "bits and pieces" programme means anything I must dispute the minister's interpretation. I have every confidence in the minister and his ability. I am not quarrelling with him. I know he is doing the best job anyone here could do in a difficult position. But it is my duty as a member to point out to the minister, who cannot possibly have a grasp of all the details of his department, that owners of machine shops, wood-working shops and so on in my riding have gone again and again to his representative in the marine building-I do not know who owns the marine building, but it has its fair share of these notorious and useless dollar-a-year men in it-time after time and have been told to fill out a form, everything from the colour of their eyes to the date their grandmother was born. And nothing happens. Yet all these lathes are standing idle; all these mechanics not doing a tap to help Canada's war effort, and power going to waste. If I am given a guarantee that they will not be discriminated against, I can give the names of people who have told me that two or three 
primary contractors in British Columbia have said, "We fought day and night, month in and month out, to get these contracts; do you think we are going to share them with you people?" The only factory at work in that entire riding, a riding with over fifty lathes standing idle, is employing three men in putting out a little brass angle. When I hear that, just because the logging camps cannot get sufficient help, because ship yards can and do pay higher wages, we have not the unemployed that we are supposed to have, I say that I cannot, and do not intend to go back to my riding and say that we have a total war effort, that we are doing our utmost to defeat Hitler, as long as there is a man, skilled or unskilled, idle in British Columbia, as long as there is power not being used that should be used, as long as there is a lathe not turning that should be turning, no matter what anyone in the minister's department says. I am firmly of opinion that it is time the minister changed his advisers in British Columbia, particularly in regard to the "bits and pieces" programme, and put in a few practical men, and I suggest that among these practical men should be a representative of labour and a representative of agriculture.

This question of labour
power is, in my opinion, going to become a difficult one before very long. This does not mean that there are not many people unemployed at present. I believe the latest figures available from the unemployment insurance commission, those for April I think, show some 35,000 to 36,000, of whom some
8,000	are women. It is not stated how many of these were employables and how many unemployables; but since these figures come from the unemployment insurance branch, I take it that only a very small number would be unemployables. There are other unemployed not in industries covered by the unemployment insurance branch. I believe the number is estimated as something over 100,000. As I said, there are no definite figures as to the number of unemployed; we are still in the same mess we have been in since 1931. It is quite possible, probably correct, that the Sitka spruce industry has difficulty in keeping their employees. That is a situation not altogether due to the better wages paid in the shipyards and other industries, although that may be a factor. If the Minister of Labour were present, he could substantiate the statement that I took up with him on, I think, the very first day he came into the house, the refusal of the employers in the logging industry on Queen Charlotte islands, where the spruce is cut, to deal or cooperate with their organized employees in any way.

War Appropriation-Supplies
The last letter I had from these employees complained that the dining-room was closed to them because they were half an hour late through attending a union meeting. Men will not stay in an industry operated on that basis when there is employment offering in other places.
I do not know whether any hon. members have ever been in the Queen Charlotte islands in the summer. It is not a nice place to work. The ground is soggy, wet; the men are walking around on wet ground all the time; there are mosquitoes and black flies, and many other things to make life miserable even if the employers did not help to make it still more miserable. It is no wonder the men leave there to work in the shipyards where they have some say as to the conditions under which they work. If this government wants to get men in the various industries and do it without having to adopt the methods of Hitler, they must do it through cooperation between employers and employees. There is no other way of doing it except the way our enemies are doing it. If we have to resort to that sort of thing we might as well stop the war, because we shall have reached the stage where our enemies were before we went into the war. I believe the director of national services, who has recently been appointed, has some good ideas in this direction; I hope he will be given an opportunity to try them out.

When I hear individual members of this committee advocating things that are regional, things absolutely of advantage to their own political security, it amazes me to think that at other times they may say that we are now undertaking a unified effort in Canada. When I hear individual members rise on behalf of local aggrandizement and undertake to carry on a campaign of belittle-ment against our Minister of Munitions and Supply, who is recognized to-day as the most proficient man in that capacity in perhaps the entire commonwealth, I do not see where our effort is so unified as some of these hon. members profess it to be. I come from a constituency in which there is not one war project. I am not protesting against that. I believe the men who are at the head of affairs, in laying out these projects, take heed of the economic and strategic factors entering into them as far as our war effort is concerned, and I am perfectly satisfied. I may not be able to judge for myself, but from what I gather, not only in Canada but abroad, our Minister of Munitions and Supply is doing a wonderful job, and I am not particularly concerned over any local grievance, or because
I cannot do something for my constituency which possibly would mean my return to parliament. I am concerned with this war effort, and I do not like to sit around and listen, and pretend to be an appreciative audience when individual members rise in their places and carry on a campaign of belittlement because certain things have not been done in their constituencies, out of the multiplicity of things that have to be done in our war effort, none of which has been done in my constituency.

I rise to a question of privilege.
I am not sure whether the last speaker intended his remarks to apply to the speech I made here this evening, but I am one of those who mentioned local matters, and I am asking the hon. member to withdraw that statement if it referred to myself. Certainly I said something about a local matter, but it was constructive. I have taken the attitude, Mr. Chairman, that we need ships now and more ships. I endeavoured to point out to the minister that the production of steel has reached a point beyond which perhaps it could not be very much expanded. I pointed out that Great Britain requires ships, if she requires anything, and I urged that wooden ships be built in British Columbia. I ask the hon. member to withdraw his statement if it applies to me, because it is untrue as far as anything political in my remarks is concerned.

My statement was
general.

I must ask for a withdrawal, too, as far as I am concerned, and it is not enough to say that the statement was general:	If the maritimes are satisfied,
we from British Columbia are not, as to Canada's war effort, as has been said before by some members from British Columbia. We are not talking for our own ridings. I have not a shipyard or anything at all in my riding, not even lobsters; I have only people who are interested in Canada's war effort, and so I ask for a withdrawal as far as my riding and myself are concerned.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think by this time the point is quite clear. The hon. gentleman did not address his remarks to any particular member of the House of Commons.
But it was evident whom he meant.
There were only three previous speakers.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. His remarks contained- a statement of fact, which has been

War Appropriation-Supplies
challenged, and I think the record speaks for itself. There was nothing in the remarks of the hon. gentleman that was unparliamentary.
I did not say there was anything unparliamentary in what he said. I said there was an innuendo; and I dispute your suggestion, Mr. Chairman, that it was a statement of fact.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
My ruling is not
debatable.
But you cannot prevent me from saying so.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. The incident is closed.
You just think it is.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I hope the hon. gentleman does not challenge the authority of the Chair, or desire to be unruly. I would simply say. that his remedy is an appeal from the decision of the Chair. My humble person is not involved; it is only my effort to be the servant of the committee in applying the rules. I am sure my hon. friend is an old enough parliamentarian to understand that.
I should like to withdraw a statement I made.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please; the incident is closed.
But I want to withdraw a statement.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
On a point of order, I want to withdraw.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order; the incident is closed.

Mr. Chairman, the question of immediate importance, in my opinion, still appears to be how we can most rapidly bring about the expansion of the production of certain war materials, such as ships, aeroplanes and tanks. To me that appears to be of greater importance at the present time than how we can expand our army overseas. I make that statement because in the theatres of war to-day the real shortage is not so much in men as in machines. For instance, in Russia they have tremendous reserves of men, but they are lacking in aeroplanes and tanks. From what we can gather, the loss of Singapore was brought about not so much by any lack of men, because apparently we had superiority in man-power over Japan, but because Japan had overwhelming air superiority. According to the statement of the editor of the Sydney Daily Telegraph, in Australia to-day there is

a corps of first-class, front-line airmen waiting for planes from America. If I were in the front line again I would far rather have a few men, well backed up by tanks and aeroplanes, than a large number of men without that support. So surely the principal question should be how we can most rapidly expand the production of these essential war materials. For that reason I take strong exception to the statement made over the air quite recently by the Minister of Munitions and Supply, when he said:
It is difficult for me to believe that many situations will arise where it can be shown, to the satisfaction of any board, that a young man cannot be replaced by industry. I appreciate the fact that newer industries, such as aircraft production, depend greatly on young men who have been trained for work in that particular industry, but I cannot support the view that industry is entitled to their services, in preference to the active service forces.
In my opinion to apply such a policy to aircraft production to-day would be criminal folly. Not long ago I was speaking to the manager of a propeller factory in Montreal. He told me that he was having great difficulty in holding his skilled men, who were being called up for service; and he pointed out that as far as propeller factories are concerned, they need a far larger proportion of skilled men than do other industries. During the Easter recess I visited a number of aircraft factories around Montreal. There is no doubt that the production of many of these factories could be greatly expanded at the present time, utilizing only the machinery they now have.
For example, the president of one of the three large plants in Montreal told me that he was very critical of the policy of the government in the past. He explained to me how at first he had been tooled up for an order of five aeroplanes, and then an order for seven planes was placed. He said that he was in the position where he had to hound the government continually for an expansion of business, whereas in his opinion it should have been the other way; the government should have been hounding industry to maintain production at the maximum level. He told me there was no trouble with labour, and he emphasized the fact that if he could have additional floor space he could double his production without any new machinery. He said that labour would be available for that purpose. I was told, on authority that I would not hesitate to accept, that the question of whether or not that floor space should be expanded depends upon whether or not sufficient business could be obtained to warrant the expansion. That is something I find it very hard to understand. A few minutes ago the minister said that we

War Appropriation-Supplies
were producing rriore than we needed in Canada for our troops. On the other hand, we are supplying planes to Russia and soon will be sending planes to Australia. Surely there is no danger of producing more planes than those people need. I cannot understand why there should be any question of whether or not we should expand the production of any plant for fear there might not be enough business to warrant that expansion.
I understand that, apart from the engines, practically all the parts which go into an aeroplane are being manufactured in Canada, and the minister has assured us that we can get enough engines to install in the planes we build. The production of planes could, no doubt, be expanded by applying the surplus labour still available for that purpose. At every plant I visited I was told that there was no shortage of labour, and I visited about nine plants in Montreal. The first question I asked when I went to a plant was: have you any trouble about labour? I was always told that there was no shortage of labour. They told me that whereas in the past forty or fifty men used to turn up every day looking for work, only ten or twelve turned up to-day. Labour would be available for that purpose. I must admit that I was very much surprised to receive that statement from the plants in view of what was said by the Minister of Munitions and Supply to the effect that our production was rapidly reaching its peak because of a shortage of skilled labour.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: My hon. friend has said that he visited a number of plants and was told that there was no shortage of labour. Will he accept a list of plants from me to visit and see what he finds there?
I visited the three large plants in Montreal: Canadian Car and Foundry, Canadian Propellers, Noorduyn and Fairchild.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: They are quite small operations. I suggest that the hon. member visit the aluminum company and the nickel company and see some larger operations.

I am talking about aeroplane plants in Montreal, not about mines. The manager of one of the main plants there emphasized the fact that he could expand the production of his plant 100 per cent if he were given additional floor space, and he could do this without additional machinery.
The international association of machine workers, lodge No. 712, have an agreement with the three main plants in Montreal. They urged the managers of those plants and Mr. Bell that they should go over to a 168-hour
production week, running three 8-hour shifts with a swing shift in order to give the men a one-day holiday a week. In order to be fair to them I should just quote from the brief which they submitted to the managers and Mr. Bell. I quote:
Accelerating the rate of present production schedules of "planes on order" is possible immediately. Our proposal that the industry chart a course to go over to the 168 hours per week production schedule (3 eight-hour production shifts per day and the seven-day working week) points the way to substantial speeding-up of the present schedules of production of "planes on order" and is also necessary to gear the industry for any contemplated upward revision of aircraft production plans by the government. To-day, we estimate that approximately 7,000 Montreal aircraft workers are engaged on the day-shift, with approximately 3,000 on the so-called night-shift. Our estimation is that Fairchilds is operating on the basis of around one and one-half production shifts per twenty-four hour day. Noorduyns about the same; that Vickers when in full production operates about the same; Federal Aircraft about the same; Aero about the same; and that the Pointe St. Charles plant of Canada Car operates between one and one-half to two production shifts per day, while their Turcot plant operates one eight-hour production shift per day.
Assuming that supply problems can be solved to bring up to assembly points all necessary material, and that cooperatively we can organize the necessary extra workers and personnel and that the plants go over to three eight-hour production shifts per day, a conservative estimate would be that production figures can be increased by at least 100 per cent upon this basis.
And again:
Personnel problems arise out of our proposal above, and it may be assumed that the gearing of our industry to the 168 hour production schedule will call for between 18,000 and 20,000 workers, that is, 8 to 10,000 additional people.
I notice that Mr. Ralph Bell gave a statement to the press in reply to that, reading as follows:-
The question of whether or not the aircraft plants in Canada shall or shall not work twenty-four hours per day, seven days a week does not depend on whether or not the men and women operating these plants are prepared to work such schedules, but rather, and entirely on two points:
1.	Whether or not it is possible to procure for expanded production schedules adequate quantities of all of the materials and thousands of parts, accessories, et cetera, of which there is already a shortage and without which the manufacture of complete finished aircraft is impossible, and
2.	Whether in an industry in which personnel has been expanded forty times in the short space of two and a half years, it is possible to develop sufficient competent superintendents, foremen and lead hands to staff three shifts, as against the two shifts on which the bulk of the Canadian industry is now being operated.
War Appropriation-Supplies

I would point out that they are not really operating two shifts because the night shift is only aproximately half the day shift, in other words they only operate about one and one-half shifts. In so far as the first part of this letter is concerned, as to whether or not we can get materials and parts for these planes, the fact is that these parts are being manufactured in Canada. We have the surplus labour, and surely it would be only a question of applying that surplus labour to the production of these parts to make them available for a larger production of planes.
The manager of Noorduyn was quite emphatic that you could get more efficient work from the men and a greater production from the plant with a five-day week for the men, keeping the plant going the full seven days. These plants are now operating a 10-hour shift and, with so many young girls working in the plants, I can easily understand why there is so much sickness. It is not easy for these young girls to stand up to a 10-hour shift. Surely by having three 8-hour shifts, we could reduce the amount of sickness and the number of absentees which is one of the curses of all industry to-day.
Apparently no steps are being taken at the present time to expand the training of men and women in order to make it possible to go on a three 8-hour shift programme. As was pointed out, that would require an additional
8,000	men. Surely, until that maximum production has been attained, there should be no question of withdrawing trained men from these industries and supplanting them with girls. In regard to the possibility of expanding production, the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maelnnis) referred to a statement in a sessional paper to the effect that 34,000 men and women were unplaced by the unemployment insurance commission. Probably most of these people will be untrained, but in view of the fact that we are approaching a crisis in which it is so essential that we have more planes, more tanks and. more ships, we should not hesitate to withdraw skilled labour from the gold mines of this country because they are certainly not essential to our war effort. The United States has classified goldmining as a non-essential industry, and I think it is high time that we took a similar stand in this country. Would the minister explain why it is not considered sound or feasible to run the various aircraft plants on a 168-hour basis?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
As I said before, the aeroplane industry is expanding very, very rapidly. Since the war began, it has been taking on men at an average rate of 2,000 men a month, but there is a limit to how fast men can be
[Mr. Queleh.l
taken on and absorbed in' an industry. Our objective is a seven-day week and three eight-hour shifts, and we have achieved that in a number of factories, also in two plants in the shipbuilding industry. But it takes a very highly organized and well-equipped plant to operate on that basis. In the first place we must have, not three shifts, but four shifts of supervisory staff to run that sort of operation. That means, of course, a great many more foremen and more supervisory staff.
There is another thing. The aircraft industry, as my hon. friend has seen it, is an assembly plant, and back of the assembly plant there are a great many factories making component parts which have to be first developed to a stage where they will permit the assembly plant to proceed on the kind of intensified three-shifts-a-day basis that he urges. I can tell him of a number of plants which have been organized to the point where they are working on three shifts a day. The Bren gun plant, for instance, has been working seven days a week, and three eight-hour shifts a day, for over a year, and I could name many more, but there you have an integrated industry where everything except the raw materials is made on the premises. It is much easier to organize that sort of plant on a high-pressure basis, seven days a week and twenty-four hours a day, than a plant which is in reality an assembly plant, back of which there are many hundreds of small shops manufacturing component parts. But we shall, I think, as time goes on, bring the aircraft industry up to that point. We have one plant that is not far away from that now. It is pretty well organized, and I think we shall eventually get the industry on a seven-day week and three-shifts-a-day basis. But it takes time. If we could stabilize the industry and say, "we will keep to the models we now have and make no further changes," and stop expanding floor space, we could bring the industry up to the stage my hon. friend suggests. But it is an expanding industry in many ways, and we have not yet reached that point.

Until we have done so
should we not hesitate to withdraw skilled labour from the industry for the army because that is bound to retard production? On the other point, that we should not hesitate to give a plant enough business to warrant an expansion of floor space, do I understand the minister to say that it does not matter whether we get the United States to buy these planes from us, to make them available to England or Russia under the lend-lease plan?

War Appropriation-Supplies

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
Not at all. There is not a
plant in Canada that has not sufficient work to last until the end of 1943.
At the present rate?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
They can produce as fast as
they like. They have ample orders. There is no restriction on anyone producing all that their plant can produce to-day. If they do not do so, they are missing a golden opportunity and are out of pocket on that account. There is no lack of orders to-day. It has taken time to organize our plants for continuous production, but there is not a plant in Canada to-day that cannot tell you what planes they are going to be making this time next year.
My hon. friend says that once a man goes into the aeroplane industry, he should be kept there and not be taken out for the army. I do not consider that a man who has spent six or eight months in the aeroplane industry is a skilled mechanic who must not be taken out of the industry for the army.
You would lose the benefit of eight months training because you would have to put a new man in the industry in his place.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
Perhaps so, but the armed
services require mechanics too. The air force, for instance, requires mechanics just as badly as does the aeroplane industry, and if they cannot get them from industry they have to train them. It is just as easy to train a mechanic in an aeroplane plant as in a training school.
The army will not need mechanics unless they get the machines from industry.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: The army is not badly off for machines to-day. It is all very well to theorize, but after all it is only fair to take an industry and see what it was a year ago and what the trend has been since then up until to-day. To-day the aeroplane industry is vastly stronger than it was a year ago or even six months ago, and a year from now when we have been able to stream-line the industry we shall have a greater ratio of employment, but as long as my hon. friend says that there is great unemployment, and keeps insisting on that, I cannot agree with him that it is improper to take men from any industry if they are needed for the army.
The minister will not dispute the figures tabled in the house by the unemployment insurance commission, which show 34,000 men and women unplaced.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: I have 34,000 jobs to-day which I cannot fill. I think we had better get together.

I think so. The unemployment insurance commission has been set up for the purpose of getting these people jobs.
The minister has referred to the fact that we have had a fairly rapid expansion of industry. I think the government are altogether too prone to emphasize the fact that the production of war materials has had to start from scratch, and that they have been handicapped by lack of skilled men, tools, plants and equipment. Whose fault was it that that situation existed? Have the men who were responsible for that position being in existence upon the declaration of war been removed from office? If they have not been, have we any assurance that they are not still to-day retarding our war effort? From 1935 to 1939 we continually hounded this government to take the necessary steps to develop the resources of this country, and members here who were in the house at that time know the kind of response we got from the Minister of Finance. Always his reply was: "There is no money available". So I think the government is not in a very good position to-day to give the excuse that it has not been able to achieve a more rapid expansion of industry because it had to start from scratch, because, in other words, it allowed the resources of this country in man-power and in industry to be systematically sabotaged during the five years preceding the war.
I should like to ask the minister two or three questions regarding the road along the Lachine canal. I have seen the Canadian Car and Foundry works, and I have seen some pretty bad roads in the west, but I have seldom seen a worse road than the particular road which is servicing that war plant. Just a week before I went there, a load of aluminum had gone over into the canal, and there have been a number of accidents. There is, I understand, a dispute between the city of Montreal and the transport department, as to responsibility for the road, but surely in a matter as important as this the government should go ahead under the War Measures Act, fix the road and argue responsibility afterwards. The road certainly should be fixed.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
That road is a private road. It is not part of the canal property. It has been a moot point. The Canadian Car and Foundry have tried to bring pressure to bear on the department from this side of the house and from the opposite side, and I am glad to
War Appropriation-Supplies

see that they have gone down now to the far comer. Nevertheless the question of responsibility has been looked into, and it is not the responsibility of the federal government. The federal government will have nothing to do with that road. The sooner the Canadian Car and Foundry Company appreciate that fact, the sooner they will get a road.

Do I understand the minister to say he is going to allow the condition of the road to impede or hamper the production of planes, as it is doing at the present time? He can take the necessary steps to see that the road is repaired, and fix the responsibility afterwards.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: I think my hon. friend would be very well advised to stick to matters he understands. He is not an engineer; he is not a highway man; he is not an expert on municipal authority, and he had better speak on more general questions.

The minister says I am not an authority on road-building. He would probably be surprised to know the amount of experience I have had, and the number of years I have spent on contract work building not only railways, but highways. I know a good deal about the condition of that road. It would not cost very much to fix. It has a hard bottom and is full of holes and ruts. He should be a little more careful about the remarks he makes when he says I do not know about roads and highways. I spent a good deal of time on subcontracts before the war.
Where?
On the Grand Trunk line, and the Goose Lake branch line, Twining and Youngstown.

Whose business is it,
anyway?
I do know that this condition is having a serious effect on our production. At the propeller factory of the Canadian Car and Foundry company there is an open sewer running right through the grounds.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: The property it is running through is owned by Canadian Car and Foundry Company Limited. I understand they are making fair returns on the contracts they have. The hon. member could suggest to them that they might fix it.

It is not their sewer. The responsibility must be with the city of Montreal or some other authority, and I think the minister should be sufficiently interested in the workers in that industry to 
see that action is taken regarding that open sewer. One can imagine what it is going to be like near that factory in the hot weather. I am not discussing whether or not it is the responsibility of the federal government or of the city of Montreal. It is near a factory engaged in producing war materials, and for that reason the minister should have an interest in the remedying of that condition.

I have understood from statements of the minister on several occasions that shortage or steel is one of his major concerns. I have a letter from H. Gauvin, manufacturer, of Ottawa, advising that:
Four million pounds of metal and five hundred thousand dollars could have been saved to date by the government on their low cost housing since the war, simply by using Enamel-Steel-Bathtubs.
I am not advertising this particular ware, but the manufacturer of these bathtubs wrote on April 1 to the director of national housing under the Department of Finance regarding this particular bathtub, and apparently it had sufficient merit to warrant a reply from the director as follows:
Having seen your new all metal bathtub I feel that it has sufficient merit to warrant us asking you for definite quotations and as discussed with you a few days ago I wish you could arrange to give us definite quotations based on:
1,000	tubs 5' long; 5,000 tubs 5' long; 10,000 tubs 5' long.
This brings me to the question I have in mind. This manufacturer was advised that Wartime Housing Limited was the department to be interested in this particular invention. The manufacturer informed me:
I wish to state that I have repeatedly offered the entire use of my patent covering my low cost enamel steel bathtub to the government for the duration of the war, with or without my services, on their own terms, for the saving of metal, with no answer.
I cannot verify that statement; but the claim that four million pounds of metal and four hundred thousand dollars can be saved would seem to me to warrant at least a reply to this letter. I took the trouble to write to Wartime Housing Limited on February 26, after giving some consideration to this man's representations, and I said to them:
Mr. H. Gauvin, 26 James street, Ottawa, has been discussing with me his Steel-Enamel-Bathtub. He discussed the use of this tub with the national housing administration here, prior to the establishing of Wartime Housing Limited, with a view to using this type of tub in the low-priced houses which were to be constructed. He has given me a copy of his file and, apparently, has not received an acknowledgment to a number of letters sent to you.
I am enclosing copies of eight letters, and would appreciate a reply from you, commenting

War Appropriation-Supplies
on this particular type of tub and whether the saving in material, which he claims would be effected, would warrant his applying for special consideration from the steel controller in connection with the manufacture of these tubs.
1 might say that, having visited the temporary houses being built by Wartime Housing Limited, it is my considered opinion that these tubs would last much longer than these temporarily built houses will last.

Are these tubs made in
Ottawa?

He had his quotation
from a reliable firm in Ottawa to manufacture in these quantities: 1,000, 5,000 and 10,000.

They are not making
them yet.

No. He has his patent, but he cannot manufacture until he gets permission from the steel controller.
I failed to get a reply from the government-owned company which has already undertaken to spend thirty million dollars of public money, so I had occasion to discuss the question with the minister. After doing so, he assured me he would get a reply, and so the day after the interview I wrote the minister as follows:
As suggested during our interview yesterday, I am writing you in connection with correspondence between Mr. H. 'Gauvin of Ottawa and Wartime Housing of Toronto, and also regarding a letter I sent to Wartime Housing on February 28 which has not been acknowledged to date.
You intimated you would find out why these letters have not been acknowledged, and let me have a report at a later date.
That letter was written on March 18, and to date I have not had a reply from the minister, so I assume that he did not have any reply from his government-controlled company, Wartime Housing Limited.
I have a letter from Mr. Gauvin, dated May 1, the last paragraph of which reads as follows:
About a month ago, a gentleman called on me saying that he represented the Wartime Housing Ltd. and wanted to inspect my Steel-Enamel-Bathtub and make a report to the Wartime Housing Ltd. I gave him all the information he wanted and he inspected the product, and it turned out he was a representative of Crane Limited acting for Wartime Housing Limited.
That is a strange set of circumstances, that Wartime Housing Limited, after this long delay, finally sends to inspect this particular bathtub a representative of a rival firm.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Might I point out that there is a difference between Crane and my hon. friend's friend, in that one makes bathtubs and the other does not. Is that not true?

Yes; but the minister is not going to laugh away this question as easily as that. I am not contending that this bathtub is everything it is represented to be, but at least I think the manufacturer is entitled to a statement from some responsible official of this government.

What manufacturer?
There isn't any manufacturer.

Oh, yes; the manufacturer is H. Gauvin, and his bathtub is available for display, I understand, if any member of parliament wishes to see it. I again wrote the minister, on May 5:
On March 18, I wrote to you following an interview on the previous day in connection with Mr. H. Gauvin.
I still have not had any acknowledgment from Wartime Housing Limited on the letter I wrote to them on February 28. Mr. Gauvin has written to me again, and I have just advised him that my letter of February 28 has never been acknowledged-
I think the people of Canada are not going to be satisfied with Wartime Housing Limited failing to answer a letter from a member of parliament regarding a claim of this sort. I merely asked them for a statement that this proposal was "all haywire" or that it had some merit in it. I have not had even the courtesy of a letter. For Wartime Housing Limited to send a representative of Crane to report on this particular project, and even after that has happened, being unwilling to reply to a member of this parliament, who in turn is responsible to the people of Canada for national expenditure, simply is not good enough. I ask the minister to tell this committee why Wartime Housing Limited cannot reply to letters of this sort and why they have to engage employees of Crane to pass an opinion on a matter of this kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Rightly or wrongly, the department takes the view that articles should be sold on their merit and that they should not be high-pressured by members of parliament. I do not like to say that to hon. members, but frankly we do not like-
High-pressured by Crane.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
-members of parliament to act as high-pressure purchasing agents. My hon. friend is very much interested in housing. I have had many talks with him about it. I asked about this project, and requested him to get a report on it himself, whether there was any merit in this thing. My hon. friend cannot demand a reply from me on behalf of the salesman of a product to the Department of Munitions and Supply. He is not entitled to do that, and he cannot demand

War Appropriation-Supplies

it of any member of my staff. It is not the privilege of members of parliament to interfere in the purchasing of the Department of Munitions and Supply, and every member of parliament knows that except my hon. friend.
I have no interest in this firm or in this individual in any shape or form.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Well, the hon. gentleman has written a great many letters about him. He is selling a commercial product to a buying . department of the government.

According to the information, he can provide-and the minister has not contradicted it-a saving of four million pounds of metal and 1500,000. That has been claimed, and a reliable firm in Ottawa has submitted quotations. According to the quotations to the national housing administration, which also is a government-owned concern, he is offering 1,000 bathtubs at $15.10 a bathtub, 5,000 at $13.90 and 10,000 at $13.15.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Was this tender accepted?

No, for the reason that he cannot get the materials until he gets permission from the steel controller. Any hon. member who will visit the houses in Hull will agree with me that $15 a bathtub is quite good enough for those houses. I cannot see any reason for the minister taking the stand he does, that a member of parliament is not entitled to a reply to letters such as I have written, as to whether there is merit in the man's claim. All I ask for is a statement to the effect that his bathtubs are not acceptable and his claims are extravagant.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: I will call my hon. friend's sales talk to the attention of my purchasing department.

That is not good
enough. On March 18 the minister took a different attitude from the one he is taking to-night. My understanding then was that my request was legitimate, and I thought I would receive the information. Would the minister tell the committee why wartime housing has refused to answer my letters in this connection? I should like to have an answer to that question.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Frankly, all I can say is I do not know why they refused. I shall be glad to ask them to give an answer.

The minister should withdraw the statement that the hon. member's speech was a sales talk. I do not think that is a dignified statement or is consonant with

the decorum of the house, and the minister certainly should not use his privilege as a minister to call the speech made by any member a sales talk. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that you demand a withdrawal of that statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: I withdraw with pleasure.

There are one or two matters to which I wish to call attention, but before I do so I would refer to a remark made by the minister in reference to the member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch). He suggested that the hon. member was overemphasizing the unemployment situation, and I think he implied that there was no unemployment problem. A return was brought down in connection with the unemployment situation. It was asked for by the member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell), and it was tabled on May 6. It had to do with the unemployment question. The first question was this:
What is the number of unemployed in each Canadian city of a population of 10,000 or over?
The answer to that question would not by any means give the total unemployment, because this was simply the unemployed registered with the unemployment commission for cities that had a population of 10,000 or over. The answer is:
Attached hereto is a statement showing applicants registered for employment on April 23, 1942, at employment and claims offices of the unemployment insurance commission in cities with a population of 10,000 or over.
The total number of unemployed was 33,449; total males, 25,277, and females, 8,172. That was simply those registered in cities with a population of 10,000 or over. The next question was:
_ How many in each of these cities are receiving direct relief?
The answer was:
No information in possession of the unemployment insurance commission.
In reply to a further question the information was given that the number of unemployed who have registered for employment is not a matter of record. There are two points there of which the minister should take note. There is a large number of available unemployed who are already registered with the unemployment insurance commission. The minister should know that over 33,000 have registered, and that only in cities having a population of 10,000 or over, so that it would be safe to say that there would be double that number if you took the country at large. I do not think the minister is aware of that situation.

War Appropriation-Supplies
Let me refer to the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence, No. 3, of the standing committee on railways and shipping, wherein the minister, speaking to the committee on the question of unemployment, is reported as follows:
As a matter of fact, gentlemen, there is no unemployment in this country. If you can show me a thousand men unemployed to-day I can tell you exactly where they can be employed at very excellent wages.
I suggest that he has been told where there is a large number of unemployed. I am sure the people registered would be exceedingly gratified to know that they will be employed at excellent wages. I continue to quote from the minister's statement:
This country is short of employment from end to end.
According to the statement, there is not a city in Canada with a population of 10,000 or over that has not some unemployed who are registered with the unemployment insurance commission, and I have them all here in detail, giving every city with a population of
10,000	or over. I think it would be of advantage to the minister to check this over if he is short of labour-and it is not only skilled labour he wants. Then I continue:
Mr. Maybank: All right.
Mr. Shaw: Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask Mr. Howe if his statement applies to unskilled as well as skilled men.
Hon. Mr. Howe: Both.
Mr. Shaw: That seems contrary to a recent radio broadcast that said-and I believe it is a censored broadcast-that unemployment in this country had increased by 5 per cent since J anuary.
Mr. Donnelly: Who said that?
Mr. Shaw: It came over CFBN-
I think that should be CFCN.
-in Calgary in a news broadcast about three weeks ago, and if that is correct, I would not say that your figures with regard to unemployment would stand up.
Hon. Mr. Howe:	If you can deliver me a
thousand men at Ottawa I will be very pleased to use them at Sudbury to-day. If you deliver me five thousand I can use them at Arvida.
Apparently the minister is looking around for men. There they are. Evidently there is lack of coordination somewhere. I am not trying to imply that the minister was insincere when he made the statement, but the evidence produced by the department itself is contrary to what the minister has in mind. I believe, as the hon. member for Acadia just mentioned, that many difficulties of which the minister is probably not aware could be straightened out. Take, for example, the road referred to. Regardless of the fact that the minister intimated that that was not his responsibility, 44561-1561
the fact remains that the poor condition of that road is definitely interfering with our war effort. The minister should take the officers of that company out and-I would go so far as to say-horsewhip them. That is not putting it too strongly when anybody stands in the way of our war effort. The minister should not dilly-dally with them; he has the authority and the power, and it is his responsibility t-o see that they produce 100 per cent.
Another matter to which I wish to refer is the matter that was brought up to-night by the hon. member for Lake Centre in regard to certain expenditures being charged up to production and consequently coming out of the public revenue. A war expenditures committee has been set up by this house this year, and there was one last year. I have said before that I think the members of that committee a year ago did a great deal of hard work and were sincere in their efforts. But if that committee had had proper facilities, I tell the minister that such a condition as was brought to his attention to-night would never have existed. I believe that every hon. member who is on that committee this year and every hon. member who was on it last year is and was endeavouring to assist the government in its war effort. Saving money was one of their major objects. This year the question of production comes in. If the committee is given every facility I believe it will greatly assist the minister. But I do not believe that the committee, as now constituted, can do that work of checking up such details as were brought to the attention of the minister to-night. The committee which sat a year ago, working as energetically as they could, did not have the legal or technical advice of men independent of the government to enable them to investigate a case like that. What should have been done is that the committee should have had a secretariat. That is, they should have been permitted to employ a man who could give them sound legal advice, a good lawyer independent of the government or of members of parliament. They should also have had at their disposal a first-class accountant and a good statistician. The minister may say, "Oh, well, you cannot spend so much money."

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
