speechtext: L)o not put words in my mouth. I am saying nothing.

I did not say the minister said it, but he looked as though he might have said it. I am not trying to attribute anything to the minister; I am suggesting that he or someone else might raise the question of expense. But the matter spoken of to-night was an excellent example:

War Appropriation-Supplies
of how a large amount of money might have been saved to the government. After all, if the employment of a secretariat such as I have mentioned would help the government save money and would in any way increase the present production of our war machine, it would be money well spent.
The question might be raised, "What do you want a lawyer for when you have several lawyers on the committee?" The subcommittee that I happen to be on is dealing with contracts and production. There are lawyers attached to the committee; but regardless of what anyone may say, there is a political tinge, and the endeavour should be to get away from politics entirely. That can be done by sitting in camera. But there must be some person who can give legal advice. On these committees are many who are not lawyers. I think a lawyer is good in his place, and that would be one place for him. Certainly the committee should have the services of an accountant. How can ordinary laymen delve into these matters and find out such a thing as was brought up to-night in regard to this morale-building matter?
The minister is missing a wonderful opportunity if he does not insist that the war expenditures committee be given a secretariat so that they can search diligently into this department. I had an example of the need the other day. I put a question on the order paper asking for the production of papers in regard to the Ottawa Car and Aircraft company. I received a telephone call from the department. Mr. Marsh informed me that there were two wheelbarrows full of correspondence-I think it was two. He said, "Surely you do not want me to copy all this and send it over to you." Well, if he had done it, I would not have had time to go through it. So I said, "No, that is not what I want." He said, "Well, if you will tell me just what you want, I will try to get it." There is the difficulty the committee will find themselves in, and that is just one small company- two wheelbarrows full of correspondence. I suggest that no committee can go into such a matter with the intention of assisting the department and thereby assisting our war effort unless they have someone that they can call upon in such matters, someone absolutely independent of the department. If such were the case now, it would be a very easy thing to say to a chartered accountant and perhaps an experienced lawyer, "Now, you fellows go into that department and get all the material we want." I am sure the department is not trying to hide anything. I am sure Mr. Marsh, who telephones me, would do his best to get the material I require, but how does he know
tMr. Johnston (Bow River).;
what we want? I believe that if the committee is to do the work it should do, it should be given a secretariat which would efficiently and effectively go into these departments and get the information we are trying to get. If you keep the committee sitting in camera it will not be a case of publicizing the thing in order to get publicity; it will be a case of doing the job efficiently. Then, when we get through, members of the committee will not have to rise in the house and say, "We did not have an opportunity to go into that department. We did not have the time, and we did not have the facilities at our disposal."

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not want to interfere with the hon. gentleman, but he is discussing a matter of procedure before a committee of parliament. I do not believe this is the proper time or place for that. The matter of procedure in a committee must be discussed in that committee. The committee may report to the house and request the remedies suggested by the hon. member, but it is not in order to discuss the procedure or the powers of a committee, or the assistance the committee should receive, when we are considering the resolution now before the committee of the whole.
I was referring to the war expenditures committee of last year, Mr. Chairman. I think that can be discussed now, can it not?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: No; this is not the proper time or place to discuss even a committee of last year.
Well, Mr. Chairman, my only desire in bringing up this matter is to endeavour to avoid a repetition of what occurred to-night.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have indicated the procedure to the hon. gentleman. I am not here to suggest ways and means, but I have indicated the procedure to which the hon. gentleman may have recourse, before the committee itself. Then, if the committee at present sitting on the very subject being discussed by the hon. gentleman-
Just what would be the procedure in the committee? Would you tell me, sir, how I could do that in the committee? What would be the procedure?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The committee itself could deal with that question. If the committee feels that it needs assistance, it is for the members of the committee themselves to discuss how they should go about getting it.

War Appropriation-Supplies

I quite agree, Mr. Chairman, that it is the privilege of any member of the committee to discuss in the committee what he thinks should be done. But even you, Mr. Chairman, I do not think would overlook the fact that with its present set-up, with a large majority of government members, it is doubtful whether the committee would accept any such suggestion.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: At the moment I am not interested in that, except to say that it would not be in order now to discuss the procedure of the committee. If, when the report of the committee is drawn up, the minority members do not feel satisfied with the procedure, they can bring in a minority report.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I venture to say that no report will be brought back to the house for some little time. I am suggesting to the minister-

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: What has the minister to do with a committee which is investigating the Department of Munitions and Supply? It is not my committee; I am not a member of it.
I think it would be to the minister's interest to suggest-

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Never mind the minister. You are a member of the committee; you do what you like. It has nothing to do with me.
Then how does the minister expect that minority members of a committee will be able to do what they like in that committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: I do not care what they do. I am not a member of the committee.

I am just about coming to that conclusion. But I think the minister would do well to demand that a secretariat be placed at the disposal of that committee, so that a proper investigation might be made of his department.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Any discussion as to
the composition of the committee is altogether out of order. This matter was dealt with when the motion setting up the committee was before the house. It is out of order to discuss either the composition or the procedure of the committee now.

I shall
abide by your ruling, Mr. Chairman, and we will do the best we can. When the report is made, we will see what can be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
A few days ago the hon.
member for Bow River brought up a subject which I would not reopen but for the fact
that I have had protests from both the management and the employees of the Calgary rolling mills because of the statements made by my hon. friend. Those rolling mills are in the constituency of Bow River, and I should think we might expect any statement made by the hon. member to be accurate. As reported at page 2028 of Hansard for April 30, the hon. member said:
Within the last little while I have heard the Minister of Munitions and Supply say there was a shortage of steel. I do not believe that.
I do not quarrel with that; I would not expect the hon. gentleman to believe me.
I think that statement is absolutely incorrect-
Again I am not surprised.
-and I am going to tell you why. The rolling mills in Calgary quit work at five o'clock every afternoon. One of the men in the factory told me that they could produce three times the supply that they are producing.
It has been brought to my attention, officially and otherwise, that since the Calgary rolling mills opened they have been working seven days a week, three shifts per day. I have the production figures of the mill from the time they started in September. They are as follows:
Gross tons
September	 1,409
October	 1,195
November	 1,455
December	 1,192
January	 1,738
February	 1,523
March	 1.644
April	 1,743
I have had the output checked by our steel expert, and I am told that this is top capacity for a mill of that size. I think, in justice to his constituents, my hon. friend should apologize to the house for a misstatement of that kind.

I have
absolutely no intention of apologizing to the house or to the minister, because I believe the statement I made will bear investigation. The minister has now gone to a great deal of trouble to investigate this situation. Why did he not do some investigating when we were pressing to have the mill opened? Surely there was enough criticism in this house about not opening it, but the minister was not in any great hurry then to open it. I want to ask the minister a question or two about the mill. I should like to ask how many blast furnaces are in operation at the mill.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Eleven o'clock.
Progress reported.
